sources.quote:
21. Donor and Upstream Applications
Where an application or component is based on, forked from, or explicitly uses another application as its donor or upstream implementation, the donor source must be treated as authoritative reference material for inherited functionality. Unless the user explicitly specifies otherwise:
1. The latest appropriate donor source should be obtained or referenced.
2. Existing donor functionality should not be recreated from memory when the actual implementation is available.
3. Relevant features, quality-of-life behaviour, keyboard interactions, menus, workflows, and expected user-facing behaviour should be preserved or appropriately adapted.
4. Proprietary functionality that cannot be reused should be replaced with a project-native equivalent where required rather than leaving an unexplained gap.
5. Required copyright notices, licences, attribution, and source obligations must be respected.
6. The relationship between the derivative implementation and its donor should remain traceable in the project's development records.

Where an app declares a donor/upstream project, the implementation MUST contain the actual donor source (forked, vendored or otherwise included according to the repository architecture) in the app’s source tree/build graph. Runtime installation MUST NOT require the user to separately download the donor application merely to obtain donor functionality. The selected donor revision/version and local modifications MUST be traceable.

The implementation MUST obtain and include the selected appropriate Avalonia source revision in the CUI source tree/build graph under the global donor-source contract. The exact upstream repository, selected revision/release, licence obligations and local modifications MUST be traceable.
CUI MUST maintain an upstream-parity manifest for the low-level Avalonia capabilities it relies on and a CUI property-parity manifest for broadly applicable visual/layout/property families derived from Avalonia and mature CSS concepts. A feature being absent from CUI's small primitive element vocabulary is not permission to omit mature framework capability when it can be represented through Type, property, Definition, Prefab or Object hosting.
The public CUI language/runtime is versioned independently from Avalonia. Upstream Avalonia changes MUST be adapted behind CUI contracts and MUST NOT silently alter public CUI syntax or semantics.

Dulche MUST carry a maintained Strata fork rather than treating a separately installed Strata application as a required user dependency. The fork MUST preserve applicable upstream and third-party licence notices, keep model-weight licences separate, and remain intentionally close enough to upstream that security, correctness and performance improvements can be reviewed and merged without repeatedly re-forking the project.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Native Home bootstrap and web service capability negotiation

sources.quote:
Every installable/native 9to1 app has a hard runtime dependency on 9-1 Home. Before initialising the app’s normal UI or opening user artifacts, the app MUST complete a local Home availability/version handshake against the Home-managed shared services it requires.


If Home is not installed, the app MUST refuse normal startup and display only a minimal bootstrap surface explaining that 9-1 Home is required. The bootstrap surface MUST provide an Install Home action that opens/starts the trusted Home installation flow. It MUST NOT create or mutate normal app data while Home is absent.


If Home is installed but the required shared service/API version is missing, incompatible or damaged, the app MUST refuse unsafe normal startup and offer the appropriate Home update/repair flow with a structured reason. Apps MUST NOT silently launch private replacement services to bypass the missing Home dependency.


This local-install dependency applies to native/installable clients. Browser-hosted web surfaces cannot require a local Home installation; they instead use the corresponding authenticated 9to1 shared web services and capability negotiation defined for web clients.

Home Core MUST expose a machine-readable service registry describing Home-owned platform capabilities and versions. At minimum it includes Dulche broker/runtime coordination, permission/trust broker, Shared Productivity Engine, package/update service, notifications, search/index, Mesh and account/session capability availability.


Before normal startup, every native 9to1 app MUST complete a compatibility handshake against Home Core and declare the required service/capability versions it needs. Missing/incompatible required services result in the global Home repair/update/bootstrap flow rather than undefined partial operation.


Service identity/version MUST be explicit; apps MUST NOT infer compatibility solely from the Home marketing version string.

The native package manifest MUST classify each stable PackageID/version as mandatory shared core, optional app, app-required dependency or optional feature dependency. The mandatory-shared rule takes precedence when a component is both shared and niche. Mandatory means installed, not eagerly started or loaded into memory. Record dependency version ranges, platform/architecture support, integrity/signature metadata, activation requirements and reverse dependencies using Home's existing package service.
The single trusted installer MUST install Home, all mandatory modules, the selected app and its app-required dependencies. Selecting a second app MUST reuse compatible shared packages. Internal platform package formats may be used; separate user-facing standalone MSIX installers for individual apps are not the distribution model. Native Windows and 9to1-OS use this contract through their supported packaging mechanisms. Browser apps use authenticated shared web services and MUST NOT require a local Home installation.
Before a niche feature needs an absent optional module, show the required component, download/storage impact and Install/Cancel controls. A cancelled or failed install preserves the user's work and intended action; retry is explicit and safe. A required dependency cannot be uninstalled while an installed app depends on it. Uninstalling an optional app preserves user artifacts and dependencies required elsewhere. Updates, repair and rollback use staged validation and atomic activation; interruption MUST preserve or recover the previous valid installation.
Opening an artifact or embedded app whose required app/module is absent MUST offer the same trusted install path, or an explicit unavailable state when installation is unsupported. It MUST NOT silently download unrelated apps, create a substitute viewer with lost capabilities, or claim a module is available solely because another Mesh device has it.
Acceptance: clean-install one chosen app without unrelated optional apps; add another without duplicated core; decline and retry a feature-module install; reject removal of an in-use dependency; interrupt an update and recover; uninstall/reinstall without losing artifacts; verify Home version negotiation and the browser/no-local-Home case.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Shared broker lifecycle, health and recovery

sources.quote: Dulche is 9-1’s shared llama.cpp-derived local model framework/runtime. One Home-managed Dulche instance serves every 9-1 app through a broker API; apps must never launch their own competing local model servers. It owns model loading, inference lifecycle, resource limits, cancellation and local capability discovery while preserving upstream provenance.

Home Core owns the single shared Dulche broker/runtime lifecycle for native 9to1 apps. It MAY host multiple logical endpoints/models concurrently subject to resource policy, but apps MUST attach to the shared broker rather than launching competing private model servers.


Home MUST expose shared Dulche service state including Starting, Ready, Degraded, Restarting and Stopped plus endpoint/model load state, resource pressure and health/diagnostic information required for recovery. Logical EndpointID/SessionID identity remains governed by the Dulche Runtime contract.


If the visible Home shell closes, Home Core MAY continue in the background. If Home Core crashes/restarts, attached apps MUST enter a degraded/reconnecting state for Home-dependent features, preserve their own user data, and reconnect to restored shared services. Apps MUST NOT launch private replacement Dulche servers during recovery.

Home Core MUST auto-start on demand or at session startup when required by installed 9to1 apps. Closing the visible Home window MUST NOT necessarily stop Home Core. Home Core shutdown is allowed only when no required dependent operation is active or when the user/system explicitly requests full 9to1 service shutdown.


Home Core persistent state MUST use crash-safe versioned storage. Corrupt or incompatible Home state MUST enter a diagnosable recovery/repair mode; Home MUST NOT silently discard permission grants, package state, device identities or other durable control-plane state to regain startup.


If a Home service fails while apps are open, dependent apps MUST receive a structured service-unavailable/degraded signal. They MUST preserve their own artifact state and block only operations that require the failed service. When the service recovers, clients reconnect/resynchronise through stable IDs/revisions rather than restarting with assumed fresh state.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Full UI/API parity and structured shared-domain contracts

sources.quote:
UI and automation MUST call the same domain operations wherever technically possible. An app MUST NOT maintain one hidden behavioural implementation for UI actions and a different incompatible implementation for API actions.


Every public API action MUST return a structured success/error result. Expected operational failures MUST NOT be represented only by free-form human text. Error results MUST include a stable machine-readable code, human-readable message, target/action identity and relevant recoverability/retry metadata.


APIs that enumerate unbounded collections MUST define pagination or streaming. APIs that can produce long-running work MUST expose request/job identity, status and cancellation. APIs that retry or can be replayed MUST define idempotency semantics so an interrupted client does not accidentally duplicate consequential mutations.


Unknown, unavailable and empty values MUST remain distinguishable. A value MUST NOT be replaced with zero, false, an empty string or an invented default merely because the provider/backend cannot supply it. Component-specific contracts such as Dulche’s null/Na distinction override this general rule where defined.

Before consumers implement against them, owners MUST publish the versioned action catalogue with exact argument/result schemas, affected stable IDs, owner/scope, required permissions, risk/reversibility, expectedRevision for writes, pagination for lists and operationId for replayable mutations. Long operations return JobID/status/cancellation and per-target outcomes. Read/search/preview/context and write APIs enforce the same current permissions; client-supplied account, Space or Burrow IDs do not grant access.
At minimum expose the UI-equivalent create/read/update/organise/delete/recover/import/export/configuration actions, Cards Rate and review queries, RevisionBank Add/Remove/Classify/Recommend/Create/Open, Sidebar AddSection/AddItem/Move/SetRule/Reset, Tabs Open/Select/Move/Close/Restore, and conversation GetPlacement/SetPlacement/SendToCloud/SendToDevice/GetTransfer/CancelTransfer. Public naming must remain within the existing canonical namespace conventions. Internal representations may vary only if these observable semantics remain compatible.
Use the existing structured error envelope. Add specific codes where absent for DependencyRequired, PackageDependencyConflict, TabTargetUnavailable, SidebarRuleInvalid, ProtectedSidebarItem, StorageModeDenied, TemporaryChatMustBeSaved, EntitlementRequired, QuotaExceeded, DeviceRevoked, TransferInterrupted, RevisionConflict, ResourceUnavailable, UnsupportedCardContent and BurrowNotFound. Errors identify action/target, retryability, retained source state and any completed/failed/skipped targets. Unknown/unavailable values are not fabricated defaults.
Persistent schemas MUST be versioned, revision-aware and crash-safe. Permission checks occur again on reconnect/commit. Repeated requests do not duplicate sets, memberships, planning items or transfers. Independent edits can merge only under the owning contract; conflicting edits preserve recoverable versions or return an explicit conflict. Normal deletion is recoverable; permanent purge remains a separate elevated operation. Migrations inspect and preserve actual existing data rather than assuming there is none.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Home permission prompts, identity and exact scoped authority

sources.quote:
9to1 Home is the central permission broker for app APIs. A caller never dispatches a protected action directly to the target app without Home first resolving its permission state. If Home is not open, 9to1 opens it and shows the approval prompt before the target action executes. A caller may submit the request to the broker, but the requested app action remains PendingApproval until Home grants it.

Values that cannot be determined without performing the action MUST be shown as unknown. requirements.requirement: P0 — Five permission decisions, trust expiry and non-overridable boundaries

sources.quote:
Prompt actions
* Decline
* Decline and Block
* Accept
* Accept and Trust
* Accept and Always Trust


Decline denies the current permission request without blocking future requests.


Decline and Block denies the request and blocks that caller from requesting or using 9to1 app API permissions until the user explicitly unblocks it in Settings. Block state is tied to the caller identity, not merely its display name.


Accept approves only the current requested action set/scope. When that request/session scope ends, later protected actions require approval again unless another trust grant applies.


Accept and Trust
Accept and Trust approves the requested ordinary action scopes and trusts that caller for 30 days. During that period, matching ordinary actions can execute without repeatedly opening an approval prompt. The 30-day trust period expires automatically and can be revoked at any time in Settings.


Accept and Trust does not automatically authorise high-risk or suspicious actions. Actions such as deleting a board, mass deleting pages/items, bulk destructive changes, changing security/permission settings, destructive account actions or similarly sensitive operations require explicit approval each time unless the caller has an applicable Accept and Always Trust grant.


Accept and Always Trust
Accept and Always Trust is intended only for software the user deliberately grants persistent trust, including self-developed scripts/apps. Within the exact granted scopes and the user’s underlying authority, it allows the trusted caller to use app APIs without routine 9to1 approval prompts, including high-risk actions explicitly covered by the grant.


Before Always Trust is granted, Home must show a prominent warning that this level of access can allow the caller to read, modify or destroy user data without asking again. The warning presents:
* Go Back
* Grant Temporary Trusted Access
* I Understand, Continue


Grant Temporary Trusted Access lets the user choose either a limited number of actions or a limited duration. The user also chooses what happens when that temporary grant ends: return to manual approval or roll down to the normal 30-day Accept and Trust level. The temporary grant must show its remaining action count/time and can be revoked early.


I Understand, Continue grants Always Trust only after the warning step. Always Trust has no automatic expiry, but remains visible and revocable in Settings.


Always Trust bypasses 9to1's routine approval prompts only. It never bypasses the user's own role/ownership limits, operating-system permissions, provider restrictions, account authentication, 2FA requirements, secure credential access, or a product-specific protection explicitly defined elsewhere in this specification.

Revocation, expiry and failure behaviour
Users can inspect, narrow, revoke and block API grants from Home/Settings at any time. Revocation applies before future protected actions are dispatched. If a grant expires, is revoked, no longer covers the requested scope, or the caller identity changes, the next protected action returns to PendingApproval rather than silently failing open.


If Home cannot display a required prompt, the action must not execute. Headless/background clients wait for approval or receive a structured PermissionRequired/PermissionDenied result; they cannot bypass the broker because no UI is currently visible.


Audit and transparency
Every API request and permission decision MUST be auditable. Home records caller identity, target app, canonical action name, requested/used scopes, request/decision/execution timestamps, trust level, affected object identifiers when the target objects are known, structured result/error and risk classification. Block, trust, expiry, revocation and Always Trust changes MUST also be logged.


The audit trail must distinguish a caller requesting an action from the target app actually executing it. Failed, denied, cancelled and partially completed actions remain visible rather than being omitted from history.

sources.quote:
9to1 MUST apply a platform-wide Privacy Ceiling baseline to every app, framework, cloud service, hosted component, telemetry path, AI feature and operating-system integration that processes personal information. Product teams MUST NOT treat privacy as an app-specific optional enhancement.


The Privacy Ceiling is derived from the strongest compatible protection required across the supported United States jurisdictions, the United Kingdom and the European Union/EEA, plus deliberate engineering headroom. The implementation MUST maintain a versioned LegalPrivacyProfile describing the currently applicable statutory/regulatory requirements for each supported jurisdiction. Where multiple requirements are compatible, the most protective requirement becomes the global default. Where applicable laws genuinely conflict, the exception MUST be narrowly jurisdiction-scoped, documented, legally reviewed and MUST NOT lower protection for unaffected users or data.


Engineering headroom means 9to1 SHOULD collect less data, retain it for less time, expose it to fewer systems, process it locally more often and encrypt it more comprehensively than the minimum legally permissible where doing so does not prevent the requested product function. A legal maximum retention period, collection scope or disclosure permission MUST NOT automatically become the product default.


Privacy by design and by default is mandatory throughout the product lifecycle. Every processing activity MUST have a declared purpose, lawful/authorised basis where required, data categories, data subjects, recipients/processors, locality/residency constraints where applicable, retention/deletion policy, access-control model and security classification. New processing purposes MUST NOT silently reuse personal data collected for an unrelated purpose merely because the data is technically available.


Data minimisation is mandatory. A component MUST request, collect, transmit, persist and expose only the personal data necessary for its declared purpose and current authorised scope. Optional analytics, diagnostics, personalisation, AI context and convenience features MUST NOT enlarge the mandatory data footprint of the core product without a separate valid basis and user/admin control where required.


Privacy-protective defaults MUST be the ordinary out-of-box state. Settings that materially broaden sharing, retention, discoverability, telemetry, cloud processing, contactability or third-party disclosure MUST be explicit and understandable. Consent or approval surfaces MUST NOT use dark patterns, misleading symmetry, preselected optional consent or unnecessarily difficult withdrawal.


High-risk processing MUST undergo an appropriate documented privacy/risk assessment before release and again after material architectural or purpose changes. The assessment MUST address foreseeable misuse, unauthorised disclosure, inference risk, vulnerable users, children where relevant, cross-border processing, AI/model exposure, account compromise, metadata leakage and recovery/incident handling.


Encryption MUST be applied in transit and at rest for sensitive personal information unless a documented technical reason makes a specific layer impossible. Where the product promises end-to-end encryption, only intended endpoint participants may possess the content-decryption capability under the declared trust model. A server-side copy of a universal decryption key, silent escrow path or moderation backdoor is incompatible with an E2EE claim unless the user-facing product explicitly describes a materially different encryption model.

Provider adapters declare credentials by reference, capabilities, privacy/residency information, rate limits and bounded backoff/retry. Model/provider fallback must be configured and permission-compatible, never silently send local/private context to a cloud. Record actual fallback models and usage. Recover with Den checkpoints; reconcile uncertain non-idempotent actions before retry.


Add Dulche.GetCapabilities(model) and endpoint capability inspection. Separate model ability, adapter/backend support, host integration and granted permissions. A supported modality grants no automatic access to microphone, camera, files, shell or network. ToolCallsAllowed = All means all tools already permitted for that caller/request. Support None, ReadOnly, selected-tool policies, scope overrides, consequential-action approval, sandboxed code and revocation.


GeneratedUI is returned as data. A CUI developer explicitly implements <GenerativeContainer> and advertises supported schemas/components/actions. Without it, retain a usable text/data fallback rather than assume rendering support. Validate components, properties, limits, references and action bindings; model output never becomes trusted executable application code. UI actions use authorised typed tools tied to the request/revision. Invalid generated UI is isolated/logged without crashing the app or losing Text.


Agents/tool loops require bounded step/time/token/cost budgets, visible progress, loop detection, approvals and cancellation. A proposed tool call is not proof of execution. Retrieved content and tool results cannot grant permissions or override the caller's restrictions.

Permissions and secrets
Authorise access per principal, namespace and object/action. Reading context, modifying an agent, executing tools and administering Den are separate permissions enforced below the UI. Revocation applies to future reads/searches/executions; it does not erase copies already disclosed.


Store credential references, not plaintext API keys, passwords, private keys or tokens in records, exports or logs. Resolve references through secure credential storage on the relevant device/service. Protect sensitive storage and transport, document key ownership/recovery and redact sensitive log payloads without falsifying whether an action occurred.

requirements.requirement: P1 — CUI direct compiler contract, vocabulary and strict syntax

sources.quote:
CakeUI (CUI) is the authoritative 9to1 user-interface framework and .cui is the only final application-markup format for first-party 9to1 applications. CUI is intentionally small, opinionated and quick to learn: ordinary application authors work with a fixed compact element vocabulary, Types, properties, Themes, Definitions, Prefabs, variables, Styles/actions and a small set of structural language constructs rather than an Avalonia-sized public control taxonomy.
CUI is derived from a pinned Avalonia source fork for mature low-level rendering, composition, text measurement, layout foundations, input, focus, accessibility, windowing and platform integration. Avalonia remains an implementation foundation; it is not the public app-authoring framework. CUI MUST compile directly to the CUI/Avalonia runtime representation and MUST NOT translate .cui into AXAML as an intermediate authoring/runtime contract.
Shipping first-party app projects MUST stop recognising .axaml and .hui as accepted application markup. C# and other implementation code remain valid for domain logic, services, specialised controls/renderers and platform integration; ordinary visible application structure and styling are authored through CUI.
The framework MUST make common UI concise without becoming ambiguous. Shorthand may reduce typing but MUST NOT change semantics or permit guessing. If a shorthand token has more than one valid resolution, compilation fails and the developer must use an explicit form.
Donor, source and compatibility contract
The implementation MUST obtain and include the selected appropriate Avalonia source revision in the CUI source tree/build graph under the global donor-source contract. The exact upstream repository, selected revision/release, licence obligations and local modifications MUST be traceable.
CUI MUST maintain an upstream-parity manifest for the low-level Avalonia capabilities it relies on and a CUI property-parity manifest for broadly applicable visual/layout/property families derived from Avalonia and mature CSS concepts. A feature being absent from CUI's small primitive element vocabulary is not permission to omit mature framework capability when it can be represented through Type, property, Definition, Prefab or Object hosting.
The public CUI language/runtime is versioned independently from Avalonia. Upstream Avalonia changes MUST be adapted behind CUI contracts and MUST NOT silently alter public CUI syntax or semantics.
Core language vocabulary
The built-in vocabulary MUST remain deliberately compact. Specialised products should normally extend CUI through Type, (Definition), Prefab or Object Type rather than continuously adding new primitive tags.

Built-in language/framework keywords are case-insensitive. User-defined IDs, Groups, C# variables, custom Definition names, Prefab IDs and other user symbols are case-sensitive unless the owning external language/package explicitly defines different rules.
Basic markup and Container types
CUI uses XML-like nesting but is its own strict language. Most behavioural variation is expressed through Type and properties rather than different primitive element names.
<Page>
    <Container Type="Grid">
        <Text>Hello</Text>
    </Container>
</Page>
Container MUST support at least Grid, Vertical Stack, Horizontal Stack and Absolute as built-in Types. Additional mature layout Types MAY be registered without changing the core element vocabulary.
<Container Type="Vertical Stack" Horizontal-Scrolling="True" Vertical-Scrolling="True">
Attribute-assignment shorthand uses a colon after an identifier. The following are equivalent when unambiguous:
<Container Type="Grid">
<Container Type:Grid>
For unquoted shorthand values, underscore MAY represent a space. Therefore Type:Vertical_Stack resolves to Type="Vertical Stack" when that is the only valid symbol. Quoted values are literal and underscore substitution never occurs inside quotes.
If both an underscored name and the corresponding spaced name exist in the active resolution scope, shorthand is ambiguous and MUST fail compilation rather than choosing one.
Comments, whitespace and escaping
Comments use <# and #> and MAY span multiple lines. Comments do not nest and do not create runtime nodes.
<# This is a CUI comment #>
Formatting whitespace outside text-bearing content is ignored. Text content uses the Text element's whitespace policy; the default collapses source indentation/newline whitespace that exists only for readable markup, while Whitespace:Preserve retains exact authored whitespace.
Quoted values are literal except for explicitly documented escape sequences. The compiler MUST provide an escaping mechanism for CUI-significant punctuation in free text/shorthand. Formatter output MUST be deterministic.

The canonical pipeline is parse -> shorthand normalization -> symbol/import resolution -> Definition/Prefab/Theme expansion metadata -> typed property/variable/action validation -> accessibility/static lint -> dependency graph generation -> compiled CUI representation/source maps -> runtime binding.
The compiler MUST NOT silently accept unknown attributes/tags/types/events/properties. Typographical mistakes such as Type:Vertcal_Stack SHOULD produce an unknown-symbol error with an unambiguous suggestion such as Vertical Stack when available.
Acceptance criteria
CUI is implementation-complete only when real compiled/runtime behaviour proves the agreed language and framework semantics. Source presence, parsing a toy file or rendering a static Button is insufficient.
Release validation MUST demonstrate at minimum:
* A real app surface authored only in .cui with .axaml/.hui rejected as app markup while using the pinned Avalonia fork underneath.
* Fixed core elements, Container Grid/Vertical Stack/Horizontal Stack/Absolute Types, scrolling and mature layout properties.
* Colon attribute shorthand, underscore-to-space shorthand, comments, strict ambiguity detection and explicit quoted disambiguation.

requirements.requirement: P1 — CUI Definitions, Imports, Prefabs and scoped identity

sources.quote:
(Definition) is a declaration modifier. A Definition creates reusable language/component definitions and is not rendered merely because its declaration is present.
<Paragraph (Definition)>
    ...
</Paragraph>
The declaration above creates a reusable Paragraph element that can later be instantiated as <Paragraph>...</Paragraph>.
<Text (Definition) Type="ABCDEFG">
    ...
</Text>
A Type Definition extends the relevant base element's registered behaviour/style contract. Built-in element and Type names cannot be silently shadowed by user definitions; an intentional framework-supported override must be explicit.
Definitions SHOULD be authored using ordinary CUI elements/properties so authors do not have to learn a separate component language.

A Prefab packages reusable shared CUI structure/code in a .cui-prefab file. Prefabs are intended for components that should be implemented once and reused across apps, such as the shared Dulche AI bar.
<Prefab (Definition) Type="static" ID="AIBar">
    ...
</Prefab>
Prefab Type MUST be static or dynamic.
* Static Prefab — all live instances share one internal mutable Prefab state. If an internal property/state changes, every live instance reflects the same shared state. Host placement, host parent, host size and host Active state remain per instance.
* Dynamic Prefab — each instance receives independent runtime state while sharing the same compiled implementation/defaults.
Static Prefab state is runtime-shared, not automatically persistent across process restart. Persistence occurs only when the owning Prefab/app explicitly stores that state.
Prefabs may contain normal elements, Definitions, nested Prefabs, variables, Styles, actions, Themes and specialised Objects. Cyclic Prefab/Definition dependencies MUST be rejected.
A Prefab exposes caller-settable inputs, actions/events and optional CUI-content/Children inputs explicitly. It MUST NOT implicitly capture arbitrary caller state.
Prefab inputs and instantiation
Prefab inputs are declared using Variable Definitions or another equivalent typed public-definition form implemented by the compiler.
<Variable (Definition) Type="string"::Title>
<Variable (Definition) Type="string"::Subtitle>
A Prefab instance may provide declared inputs in markup or runtime load arguments. Static Prefabs MUST reject conflicting per-instance mutable input semantics that would violate their shared-state contract; content requiring independent mutable state uses a dynamic Prefab.

ID and Name are aliases for the same unique identity mechanism. An element may own zero or one ID/Name and any number of Groups. Multiple elements may belong to the same Group.
<Text ID="txt" Group="Labels,Important">Hello</Text>
<Text Name="txt">Hello</Text>
ID shorthand is :: and Group shorthand is :::.
<Text::txt:::Labels,Important>Hello</Text>
Within a scope, IDs are unique. Groups intentionally contain multiple members. An ID and Group MUST NOT use the same identifier in one scope because direct runtime addressing would be ambiguous.
Generated/runtime handles allow direct element mutation:
txt.Text = "Hello";
Labels.Color = "Green";
A direct Group operation broadcasts to every current compatible member in scope. The runtime MUST validate the entire target set before a persistent group mutation; incompatible required targets cause the operation to fail rather than silently producing partial state.
ID and Group scope
Page creates a top-level CUI addressing scope. Each dynamic Prefab/custom Definition instance creates a child scope for its internal IDs/Groups. A static Prefab has one shared internal state scope. Bare IDs/Groups resolve only in the current scope; cross-scope access must explicitly name the containing Page/Prefab instance.
Groups are dynamic: active or inactive members remain members while the corresponding object exists. Persistent active Styles targeting a Group apply to newly loaded compatible members while that Style remains active.

The CUI toolchain automatically indexes supported local .cui, .cui-theme and .cui-prefab files within the declared project/source roots. External/shared packages use Import.
<Import Source:"package/path">
Ambiguous symbols from multiple imports MUST fail until disambiguated, including by an explicit alias such as As:SharedUI. Circular Definition/Prefab import dependencies are rejected.

requirements.requirement: P1 — CUI reactivity, static snapshots, conversions and Input write-back

sources.quote:
Ordinary application variables remain ordinary implementation-language values. CUI reactivity is attached to the CUI reference by default; application authors do not have to wrap every value in a special Live<T> type merely to update UI.
string Name = "Jacob";
<Text>Hello <:Name:></Text>
<:Name:> is the compact live variable-reference form. Live is assumed unless static is explicitly requested.
<:Name:live>
<:Name:static>
Typed/conversion shorthand prefixes the target type:
<int:Age:>
<int:Age:static>
The long conversion forms are equivalent:
<Variable.ToInt>Age</Variable>
<Variable Type="int">Age</Variable>
Variable.ToInt and Variable Type="int" MUST resolve to the same typed conversion operation. Equivalent ToString, ToFloat, ToBool and other registered conversion forms MAY exist. Conversion failure MUST return/produce a defined typed validation/conversion error; it MUST NOT silently substitute an unrelated default such as zero.
Live versus static references
A live CUI reference subscribes to the referenced CUI-visible value and automatically reevaluates the dependent UI when that value changes. A static CUI reference evaluates on load/explicit refresh and does not update merely because the source changes.
Static subexpressions retain their last evaluated value even when another live reference in the same element causes an unrelated update. Element.Refresh() explicitly reevaluates the element's static references; refreshing a Container/Page recursively refreshes the applicable active subtree.
CUI build tooling MUST instrument or generate change-notification plumbing for CUI-visible persistent fields/properties/observable collections referenced live. Per-frame polling is prohibited. Short-lived method locals cannot become magically persistent observable state after their scope ends.
Live dependency relationships
new Live(...) is reserved for relationships between application values/objects, not for basic CUI binding.
Graph = new Live(x, y);
The declaration above means Graph depends on x and y. A change to either dependency invalidates/recomputes Graph through Graph's defined derived getter, refresh/update operation or explicitly supplied recomputation function. Live MUST NOT invent a new scalar value when no recomputation semantics exist.
Dependency cycles MUST be rejected at compile/build time when statically discoverable and surfaced as typed dependency errors otherwise.

Displaying a variable is one-way by default. Writable Input properties bind two-way by default when the source is writable and the conversion is valid.
<Input Type:Text Value=<:Name:>>
<Input Type:Checkbox Checked=<:Enabled:>>
<Input Type:Slider Value=<:Volume:>>
WriteBack=False disables automatic source update. A :static reference is snapshot-only and has no automatic write-back.
When typed conversion fails during input, the control retains the invalid entered representation and exposes validation error state; the source variable is not overwritten until conversion succeeds.

sources.quote:
Text and Children runtime content
Text and Children are distinct runtime surfaces.
* Text is literal textual content. Assigning markup-looking characters to Text displays them as text.
* Children is structured CUI child content. Assigning to Children parses the value as a CUI child fragment under the host's allowed component/action capabilities.
Assignment means Replace by default; Replace() is the explicit equivalent and Add() appends.
txt.Text = "Hello";
txt.Text.Add(" world");
txt.Children = "<$Color:Green>Hello</$>";
txt.Children.Add("<Text>Another item</Text>");
A failed dynamic Children parse/validation MUST leave the previous valid child tree intact and return a typed error.
Active, Hidden and Interactive
Active, Hidden and Interactive are separate properties and MUST NOT be collapsed into one Avalonia visibility/enabled flag.
* Active=True means the element/declaration participates in its normal active lifecycle/tree. Active=False deactivates/unloads it from normal layout/render/input participation while retaining enough object/state information for later reactivation.
* Hidden=True suppresses visual rendering only. A hidden active object still occupies layout, retains state and can receive interaction/events when Interactive=True.
* Interactive=False disables user-originated interaction/focus targeting while leaving the active object visible/layout-participating unless another property changes that.
All objects default to Active=True, Hidden=False and Interactive=True unless a Definition/Type/Theme explicitly defines another default.
<Text::Txt Active="False">Hello</Text>
Txt.Active(true);
Active(false) is an effective participation gate and MUST NOT overwrite stored Hidden, Interactive or other properties. Reactivating restores those stored properties exactly. Property assignments made while inactive update stored state and become effective when reactivated.
Parent lifecycle and independent activation
Normal descendants inherit Active state from the nearest active parent. Effective Active is Self.Active AND parent EffectiveActive.
A leading ! or ActiveIndependently=True breaks only the parent-to-child Active dependency.
<!Style::PersistentStyle>
<Text ActiveIndependently="True">...</Text>
An independently active child/declaration is not forced inactive when its parent deactivates and must be deactivated separately. ! does not break Theme inheritance, symbol scope, Prefab ownership, variables, Groups, styling inheritance or event targeting.
For independently active visual descendants whose logical parent deactivates, the runtime preserves the required logical/positioning reference state without causing the inactive parent to re-enter ordinary sibling layout.
Lifecycle events
Initial activation generates Loaded. A False-to-True Active transition generates Loaded again. A True-to-False transition generates Deactivated. Event processing is typed and follows the ActionEvent rules below.
Stateful/non-once events are temporary overlays for the event lifetime; Once-prefixed variants commit their property/action result as persistent state rather than reverting with event end. Once means committed/persistent, not 'execute only once ever'.

Condition is live by default. When the condition changes, the applicable branch is instantiated and the other branch is removed from the structural tree. A static condition reevaluates only on explicit containing-scope refresh.
Structural removal is stronger than Active inheritance: an ActiveIndependently child cannot remain alive after the entire conditional branch that owns it ceases to exist.

<Repeat Source=<:Users:> As:user Key=<:user.ID:>>

</Repeat>
Key may be omitted only when each item exposes an unambiguous stable ID. A live Repeat without stable identity MUST fail rather than recreate items with ambiguous state transfer. The iteration variable exists only inside its Repeat instance.

requirements.requirement: P1 — CUI mature layout, coordinate modes, layers, modals and placement

sources.quote:
CUI's property catalogue MUST provide mature visual/layout coverage comparable in scope to broadly applicable CSS and Avalonia properties while retaining CUI's typed semantics. Layout is property-driven.
Required layout/property families include:
* Width, Height, MinWidth, MaxWidth, MinHeight and MaxHeight.
* Margin, Padding, CellMargin and CellGap.
* HorizontalAlignment, VerticalAlignment, wrapping/overflow and scrolling properties.
* Grid Rows, Columns, RowSizes, ColumnSizes, Row, Column, RowSpan and ColumnSpan.
* Absolute X/Y positioning and associated coordinate modes.
* Typography, colour, background, borders, corner radii, opacity, clipping, transforms, shadows/effects and other applicable mature property families.
Numeric layout units MUST be typed. Bare fixed dimensions use CUI logical/DPI-aware pixels unless the property explicitly defines another unit. Auto, percentages and fractional/fill sizing are supported where meaningful.
ColumnSizes:1fr_2fr_200
RowSizes:Auto_1fr
Grid and stack behaviour
Container Type:Grid performs row/column layout. Container Type:Vertical_Stack and Horizontal_Stack perform ordered stack layout. CellGap controls spacing between grid/stack cells/items; CellMargin controls the per-cell/item margin contribution.
Scrolling is orthogonal to layout Type and can be enabled independently.
<Container Type:Vertical_Stack Horizontal-Scrolling:True Vertical-Scrolling:True>
Invalid layout-property combinations MUST fail at compile time when statically knowable or return a typed runtime layout error when dynamically introduced.

Container Type:Absolute enables free child positioning. Bare X and Y use CUI's proportional coordinate system by default and MAY be decimal values.
The centre of the positioning surface is (0,0). The normal horizontal range is -1000 at the left edge to +1000 at the right edge. The normal vertical range is -1000 at the bottom edge to +1000 at the top edge. Values outside the normal range are legal and place the reference point beyond the surface, which is useful for transitions/off-screen UI.
<Container Type:Absolute>
    <Text X:-500.5 Y:250.25>Hello</Text>
</Container>
An axis may alternatively use X-px/Y-px for CUI logical pixels or X-%/Y-% for percentage positioning. Percentage 0 is left/bottom, 50 is centre and 100 is right/top. Coordinates in every mode MAY be decimals.
An element may define only one authoritative positioning mode per axis at a time. Supplying X and X-px together, for example, is an error.
Coordinate recalibration and inherited axes
X-Inherited and Y-Inherited independently recalibrate descendant coordinate resolution to the declaring Container's bounds.
* X-Inherited=True makes that Container's left/right bounds the descendant -1000/+1000 X range and the corresponding percentage/pixel reference surface.
* Y-Inherited=True makes that Container's bottom/top bounds the descendant -1000/+1000 Y range and the corresponding percentage/pixel reference surface.
The nearest applicable inherited axis scope wins. X and Y may therefore resolve against different ancestor Containers. Outside an Absolute/free-positioning context, free X/Y placement is invalid unless the owning specialised Type explicitly declares support.
Layering and rendering depth
Layer is both a container element and an inheritable signed-integer property.
<Layer Layer="1">...</Layer>
<Layer:2>...</Layer>
<Text Layer="5">Hello</Text>
Higher Layer values render/hit-test above lower values; negative and positive values are valid. An element-level Layer overrides the parent layer and becomes the inherited layer for its normal descendants unless they override it again. Equal layers use normal tree/source order, with the later item above the earlier item where they overlap.
Layer controls depth only; it does not by itself imply modal behaviour or layout.
Modal behaviour
Modal is a separate property. Modal=True traps applicable focus/input inside the modal subtree and blocks lower-layer interaction in the same render surface until dismissal. Nonmodal high-layer popups may sit above content without blocking unrelated lower-layer interaction outside their bounds.
Anchor and runtime placement
Anchor is an optional named placement point, not a prerequisite for loading a Prefab or dynamically created UI.
<Anchor::bob>
Runtime placement MUST support at least:
* LoadAt(anchor) — place at an Anchor.
* LoadAt(x,y) — fixed proportional coordinates in the selected/current Absolute coordinate scope.
* LoadAtPixels(x,y) and LoadAtPercent(x,y).
* LoadUnder(element), LoadAbove(element), LoadLeftOf(element) and LoadRightOf(element).
* LoadIn(grid,row,column, optional spans/alignment).
* LoadInto(container).
Relative placement operations such as LoadUnder, LoadAbove, LoadAt(anchor) and LoadIn(grid,...) remain live placement relationships and track target movement/resizing. Raw coordinate placement is fixed in the chosen coordinate scope unless the caller changes it.
When multiple Prefabs/UI instances are loaded at the same Anchor without another placement rule, they flow downward from that Anchor in load order. Raw repeated coordinate loads overlap unless another rule is supplied.

* Absolute decimal ratio coordinates, x/y pixel and percent modes, X-Inherited/Y-Inherited recalibration and nested independent axis scopes.
* Prefab/UI placement at Anchor, raw coordinates, pixels, percentages, above/below/left/right of elements and Grid positions, including live relative tracking.

requirements.requirement: P1 — CUI property precedence, Style/events and typed async actions

sources.quote:
Properties are strongly typed registered CUI properties. The long Property form and compact $ form are semantically equivalent.
<Property="Color" Color="Green">...</Property>
<$Color:Green>...</$Color>
<$Color=Green>...</$Color>
The short closing form </$> closes the most recently opened property region when nesting is unambiguous.
<$Color:Green>Hello</$>
A property region is a typed property scope, not an ordinary visual element. It can have an ID or Groups using the same shorthand system.
<$Color:Green::pinkText>Hello</$>
<$Color:Green:::greenText>Hello</$>
Multiple property declarations may contribute different property types to the same Group. If a target Group exposes exactly one property type, a property mutation may omit the property name. If multiple property types are available, the property name is mandatory.
Property-target mutation directives
CUI markup may mutate an existing property target/Group declaratively.
<:::$greenText.Color="Pink">
<:::$greenText="Pink">
The second form is valid only when greenText resolves to exactly one property type. For a multi-property Group such as Color plus Background, the explicit property is required.
<:::$fancyText.Color="Blue">
<:::$fancyText.Background="Black">
Outside a Style/event rule, a mutation directive executes when its containing declaration becomes active/loaded and executes again on later reactivation. It is a persistent stored-property mutation, not an automatically reversible Style overlay.

Style and property precedence
Effective presentation MUST resolve deterministically in the following order from lowest to highest precedence:
* CUI built-in property default.
* Inherited Theme.
* element Type/(Definition) default.
* explicit instance property.
* scoped <$Property> region.
* active Style/event overlay.
A direct runtime property assignment changes the stored explicit property value at its normal level; it is not an invisible new top-level precedence layer. If a temporary event Style currently overrides that property, the new stored value becomes visible when the temporary overlay ends.
Style rules and ActionEvent
Action events use the long form <ActionEvent Type="..."> or & shorthand.
<&Hover>
<&Clicked>
<&PointerEnter>
<&PointerExit>
Inside a Style, an ActionEvent begins a rule and following property/action declarations belong to that event until the next ActionEvent or the end of the Style. A property declaration before any event is an unconditional Style property while that Style is active.
<Style>
    <&Hover{::button}>
    <$Color:Pink{::label}>
    <$Background:Black{::label}>
</Style>
Event target syntax
Curly braces declare an explicit target. {::foo} targets ID foo; {:::foo} targets Group foo. TargetID and TargetGroup are the verbose equivalent attributes.
<&Hover{::greenText}>
<&Hover TargetID="greenText">
<$Color:Pink{:::labels}>
<$Color:Pink TargetGroup="labels">
When an event/property declaration is owned by an element/Style and no explicit target is provided, it targets the owning element/context according to that construct's standard rule.
Temporary versus Once events
Stateful events such as Hover apply their associated Style overlay only while the state is active; ending Hover automatically reveals the previously effective values. OnceHover commits the resulting mutation so it remains after Hover ends.
The same temporary-versus-committed distinction applies to corresponding event families such as Clicked/OnceClick, Loaded/OnceLoaded and Deactivated/OnceDeactivated where meaningful. Once-prefixed events may execute on later qualifying occurrences; 'Once' denotes committed effect semantics, not a one-time lifetime subscription.
Event source, propagation and cancellation
Events target the actual originating element by default and do not automatically bubble through every parent. Bubble=True enables supported upward propagation.
Event context MUST expose at least Event.Source, Event.Target, Event.Type and applicable Event.Value. For a Group trigger, Event.Source identifies the particular Group member that generated the event, enabling a single Group rule to affect only that member when desired.
Event.Cancel() cancels further compatible propagation/action when the event family permits cancellation.
Typed actions and asynchronous work
ActionEvent MAY invoke a named typed application/domain action in addition to Style/property changes. UI actions MUST converge on the same domain operations used by the app's API/Automation surface where an equivalent operation exists; CUI MUST NOT become a parallel private business-logic layer.
<&Clicked{::SaveButton} Action:SaveDocument>
Long-running/async actions MUST NOT block the UI thread and must expose typed running/completed/failed/cancelled state/events usable by CUI.

Themes and inherited theme structure
Theme is an inherited visual-design scope. Everything within a Theme uses that Theme until a descendant Theme overrides it; after the descendant closes, inheritance returns to the parent Theme.
Built-in Theme names:
* Professional.
* Glow.
* Playful.
* Bubble.
* Cinematic.
Themes are complete visual systems, not colour-only palettes. They MAY define typography, colours, surfaces, spacing defaults, control shapes, corner treatment, elevation/shadow, interaction states, animation defaults and other presentation properties, but they MUST NOT silently change the fundamental semantic meaning of controls.
<Theme Name="Glow">
    <Container Type:Vertical_Stack>
        ...
    </Container>
</Theme>
Home user-preference theme binding
CUI MUST accept the reserved dynamic theme-name input `user_preference` in any valid Theme scope, for example `<Theme Name="user_preference"> ... </Theme>`. `user_preference` is a resolver/reference, NOT a sixth built-in theme or a literal visual style. Its resolved value is the currently effective Home-managed theme selection for the active user/profile, including supported installed custom themes. Resolution MUST use the canonical Home Core settings/theme service; app-specific hard-coded theme copies, duplicated preference stores and silent overrides are prohibited.
Unless a particular nested region explicitly chooses another supported Theme, first-party 9to1 app shells and shared CUI components MUST inherit the user's effective preferred theme consistently (including Picture, Wave and Motion). An explicit descendant Theme override remains scoped and retains the documented parent-theme inheritance when it ends; app-specific temporary/preview overrides MUST be visible and reversible, must not overwrite the user's Home preference, and must not silently disable user-selected accessibility settings. Dynamic binding is reactive: valid Home changes update affected active windows/surfaces and future launches coherently, with theme resource and inherited properties re-resolved rather than merely changing accent colours.
CUI/theme acceptance MUST exercise switching Home's preferred theme among Glow, Professional and a supported custom theme, applying `Name="user_preference"` in at least two independent running apps, observing correct live/restored styling across restart and signed-in supported surfaces, then testing offline cached preference, missing/invalid custom theme fallback, descendant explicit override and return to parent preference, plus reduced-motion/contrast/accessibility inheritance. Theme updates MUST NOT change user content or canonical artifact state.
Users can define custom Theme types in .cui-theme files.
<Theme (Definition) Name="Rainbow" Inherits="Professional">
    <Button (Definition)>
        <# Theme-specific Button properties #>
    </Button>
</Theme>
Within a Theme definition, an element Definition without Type defines that Theme's default presentation for that element. A Definition with Type defines the Theme presentation for that element Type. Custom Themes SHOULD inherit another Theme when only deltas are needed.
Default typography
Montserrat is the default CUI/9to1 interface font wherever technically available and legally redistributable. First-party 9to1 applications and the 9to1-OS shell SHOULD inherit the global CUI typography system rather than independently selecting unrelated UI fonts.
CUI MUST define a robust fallback font stack for environments where Montserrat is unavailable and must support specialised font roles such as monospace/code text. Users may override the system/interface font through the supported customisation/theme framework without requiring application-specific hacks.

Home Settings → Appearance/CUI MUST let the user select their preferred complete CUI theme (Professional, Glow, Playful, Bubble, Cinematic or an available compatible custom theme). Home owns the validated, versioned user-preference setting and exposes it via the canonical Home Core settings service and authorised typed get/set/subscribe APIs. Preference scope MUST be explicit: device-local when unauthenticated; when signed in, the applicable user/account preference MUST be available consistently to the user's supported 9to1 apps and devices via normal authorised settings synchronisation, without merging unrelated users' or organisations' preferences.
Changing the preferred theme in Home MUST propagate to compatible running 9to1 app windows and newly opened app surfaces without requiring each app to implement its own theme picker, persist a competing selection or restart where live retheming is supported. Apps MUST render the effective preference through shared CUI theme resolution, honour accessibility/reduced-motion settings, and retain the selected theme across app closes/restarts. Offline clients use their last valid locally cached preference; when no valid preference or theme exists, fall back deterministically to Professional and surface any unavailable custom-theme selection honestly.

First-party compiled .cui, Plugin CUI and Generative UI are different trust classes.

Static syntax/type/property/binding errors are build/compile errors with file, line and column diagnostics and, where safe, suggested corrections.
Runtime failures from dynamic CUI, plugin content, specialised Object hosts, data or async actions MUST be isolated at the nearest declared/default error boundary where feasible so one failed component does not unnecessarily destroy the entire window/application.
An invalid dynamic CUI update must preserve the last valid tree/content. Unknown incompatible compiled CUI/runtime versions fail with a structured compatibility error.
Hot reload and developer tooling
CUI tooling MUST include compiler/build integration, formatter, linter, hot reload, component/Prefab preview, semantic tree inspector, accessibility inspector, binding/variable dependency inspection, Theme/resource inspection and rendering/performance diagnostics.
Hot reload preserves the current valid runtime tree when edited CUI is invalid. Once valid again, compatible nodes are patched while preserving state by stable IDs where unambiguous. Definition/Theme/Prefab changes update compatible live instances without arbitrarily resetting unrelated runtime state.
Testing and semantic selectors
CUI MUST expose a semantic test/accessibility tree so automated tests can locate elements by ID, role, accessible name and other stable semantic selectors rather than raw screen coordinates when semantic targeting exists.
The test harness MUST be able to render a CUI Page/Prefab at declared dimensions, Theme, scale, accessibility/reduced-motion settings and platform capability profile; interact through semantic input; inspect resulting state; and capture deterministic visual evidence where applicable.

Native CUI applications depend on the compatible Home-managed CUI/shared runtime under the global Home runtime-dependency contract. The CUI compiler/toolchain belongs to the development/build environment; the runtime version/capability requirement is recorded in app/package metadata.
Web CUI MAY use a browser-specific implementation/runtime, but it MUST preserve the same public CUI semantics, component contracts, state identities and supported action/property behaviour except for explicitly declared platform capability differences.

The Universal Model Picker is the single shared model/provider selection and routing interface for the 9to1 ecosystem. On Windows/regular 9to1 it is hosted by Home; on 9to1-OS the same canonical state is surfaced by the OS. Apps, Agents and AI surfaces MUST NOT create incompatible private model pickers, provider registries or fallback logic when this shared capability applies.
Compact picker and full manager
The compact picker is used inside apps, Agents and AI surfaces when selecting the effective model/route. The full manager lives in Home/Settings → AI/Models and adds provider configuration, installation/acquisition, aliases, defaults, route ordering, background routing, fallbacks, privacy, resource and lifecycle controls.
Entries expose stable Dulche model identity plus user-facing name/alias, provider/source, local/cloud/remote state, modalities/capabilities, tool/structured-output support, reasoning controls, context/output limits, loading/availability, privacy/residency, entitlement/cost where known and local RAM/VRAM fit where meaningful. Display names are never used as canonical identity.
Simple defaults and capability categories
The normal picker keeps the primary capability configuration approachable: Chat Model/Route, Image Model/Route and Voice Model/Voice. Advanced exposes Audio Model/Route and Video Model/Route. The user may instead choose one Active Model/Route and allow all compatible capabilities to inherit it, with ordered fallback resolving unsupported capabilities.
Chat is the primary general-purpose route for conversation, reasoning, writing, coding, tool use, agentic work and multimodal chat where supported.
Image supports an explicit Inherit from Active/Chat route. Inheritance means use that ordered route and its native image-generation/editing-capable candidates; it MUST NOT silently substitute an unrelated unconfigured image provider. A dedicated Image route is an explicit override.
Voice is the first-class conversational/live-voice selection used by Vision & Voice for supported Conversational, Monologue, Live Listener and Live Translate modes. When the selected Voice Model exposes named voices, the user-facing field is labelled Voice and selects VoiceID while showing VoiceModelID as secondary metadata. Advanced Audio covers dedicated transcription, synthesis, audio understanding/transformation or music/audio generation where applicable. Advanced Video covers video generation, editing/transformation or video-native understanding. These category routes may inherit the Active route or use explicit independent ordered routes.
Active and Background routes
Users may configure a single Active Model/Route for all foreground AI work or assign capability-specific/app/Agent overrides. Separately, a Background Model/Route can be configured for non-interactive work such as background summarisation, indexing/classification, Background Learning processing, permitted Automations AI work, proactive suggestions and other low-priority background tasks.
If no Background route is configured, background work inherits the Active route subject to normal capability/privacy/policy filtering. A task-specific explicit model outranks Agent/app/category defaults; a configured Background route applies only to eligible background work and MUST NOT override an explicit Agent/task requirement.
Ordered Model Routes
Home/Dulche MUST support versioned ordered Model Routes shared by regular 9to1 and 9to1-OS. A Model Route is an ordered list of stable configured model identities plus per-entry enabled/disabled state and routing policy. Users can reorder candidates directly in Home, including by drag/reorder UI, without changing the models' canonical identities.
Example: an Active route may be ChatGPT 6 Sol → Gemma 4 → Fable 5. The ordering means use the highest-priority candidate that is both eligible and available for the request. These operations use Dulche Runtime/Den and provider/package APIs rather than a second model-host implementation.

A turn limit, completed subtask or initial artifact is not overall completion. Continue towards the agreed outcome, not an expanding backlog of invented features or endless optional polishing.

While a Persistent root request is active, ordinary user messages sent through the same compose surface are SteeringMessages belonging to that root request. They are appended durably, ordered by receipt sequence and presented to the orchestrator at the next safe planning boundary without terminating the current turn. They MUST NOT be implemented as ReplacePrompt or StopResponse, and MUST NOT cause already completed actions to replay.
Persistent orchestration MUST maintain a dependency-aware work graph. A structured Blocker marks only the work nodes that depend on it. When a blocker needs user action or permission that the agent cannot obtain itself, Dulche surfaces the blocker and continues every runnable node that does not depend on it. If all remaining nodes are blocked, the root state becomes AwaitingUser; AwaitingUser is non-terminal and keeps recovery/checkpoint state until the user resolves, changes or explicitly stops the task.

6. Status, stages and estimates
WORKING — Substantial work is actively progressing.
STALLED — An unexpected problem is being worked through without requiring human intervention.
NEEDS INPUT — A decision or permission is needed for part of the task; other substantial work continues.
BLOCKED — Substantial remaining work cannot proceed until a person resolves the identified gate.
CHECKPOINT — A significant milestone has been reached; expose its deliverable where applicable.
COMPLETED — All agreed work is produced; verification is not yet fully satisfied.
VERIFIED — All agreed work is produced and every acceptance test passes for the current result.
Keep execution state, activity stage and milestone events distinct. For example, a task may be WORKING at the Verifying stage while reporting a CHECKPOINT and NEEDS INPUT for later deployment. A checkpoint or completed component does not imply overall completion.
Show current activity, latest meaningful result, next checkpoint, outstanding input and rough time to the next checkpoint, COMPLETED and VERIFIED. For STALLED, also estimate return to WORKING. Use ranges and update estimates when evidence changes; show unknown or conditional on input when a credible estimate is unavailable. Do not turn estimates into promises or derive progress from a running timer.


7. Verification-first completion
Verification is a default, first-class part of execution, not a separate request or optional final message. Before declaring work finished, visually inspect its rendered interface/output and test real intended workflows using the actual artifact or build. Non-visual work requires appropriate direct checks; a build passing or code looking plausible is not proof of the requested behaviour.
If a test fails, diagnose, repair and rerun affected checks and relevant regression tests autonomously until all pass. Continue within the agreed scope, permissions and resource limits. Unavailable verification remains visibly outstanding and may cause NEEDS INPUT or BLOCKED; never fabricate evidence, silently waive tests or claim success.
Record the current artifact/build revision, test result and supporting observation, screenshot or tool output. Invalidate affected results after changes. COMPLETED is an intermediate green-tick state; the default finished handoff is VERIFIED, with a gold tick, delivered artifacts and inspectable evidence. A user-directed stop may leave unverified work but must not be described as verified.

Show the objective and scope, rough overall percentage, implementation versus verification progress, current stage, elapsed time, estimates, detailed checkpoint progress, remaining work, dependencies, blockers and outstanding input. Remaining work includes implementation, integration, visual review, tests, repairs, authorised delivery and reporting, not just the agent's original checklist.
Base the approximate percentage on the agreed work and verification remaining, with reviewable checkpoint weights. Do not use time elapsed, lines changed, tool calls or checkpoint count alone as completion. Re-estimate visibly when scope or evidence changes; explain uncertainty and reserve overall 100% for a fully verified result.
Each checkpoint shows its name, status, duration, current activity, remaining subtasks/dependencies, associated tests, evidence and outputs. Completed checkpoints use a green tick; verified checkpoints use a gold tick. Active work uses a clock/progress indicator and pending work a hollow marker. Always include text labels so colour is not the sole distinction.
Example checkpoint list
✓ Forked RNote (5min 10s | Completed)
✓ Implemented Writing Engine (20min 42s | Verified)
◷ Developing APIs (1hr 20min 3s | Verifying)
○ Publish App (Up Next)
○ Progress Report (Pending)
Durations come from recorded task/checkpoint events, not model estimates. Completed durations are fixed; active durations update. Distinguish wall-clock elapsed time, active work and waiting time; do not add parallel worker durations together as overall elapsed time.
Provide expandable checkpoint detail, worker activity, action history, artifacts and a detailed diff view against a stated baseline. Use text/code diffs and suitable content/visual change views for other artifacts; unsupported diffs must be labelled, not fabricated. Keep steering, pause/resume, cancellation and input/approval controls in their appropriate dashboard surfaces.


User-added acceptance tests
Users can add tests to the task or an individual checkpoint from the dashboard at any time. Each test records a short requirement, an observable pass condition, its result, current evidence and the result revision. Show PASS, FAIL, NOT RUN, RUNNING, BLOCKED or STALE as appropriate; only PASS satisfies a test.

A newly added unsatisfied test reopens relevant verification, including after an earlier VERIFIED state. Preserve test history and make any stale gold-tick status visibly pending re-verification.
The agent must not silently delete, weaken or mark tests passed to finish. Verification is complete only when every default and user-added acceptance test passes for the current task/output revision; missing, stale, blocked and unevaluated evidence do not count.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Coordinated Subagents identities, context and actual scheduling

sources.quote:
Subagent is the Dulche Runtime term for a child execution unit created by a request or another Subagent to delegate work and/or execute independent work in parallel. Subagents are execution primitives, not persistent Dulche Agents and not Den-backed Agent definitions. The public API MUST use the names Subagent and Dulche.Subagent for this capability so callers cannot confuse subagent parallelisation with persistent Agents.


A Subagent MAY execute one or more model/tool steps and MAY create nested Subagents within inherited limits. Every Subagent belongs to exactly one RootRequestID and, except for root execution, exactly one parent request or parent Subagent. Detached/orphan Subagents are outside the current contract; child work MUST remain causally attached to its parent tree.

Start creates one child and returns its handle after identity/state allocation. StartParallel submits the supplied definitions as sibling children under the same parent and returns one handle per child in input order. StartParallel grants permission for concurrent scheduling; it does not guarantee simultaneous execution when endpoint, provider or resource limits require queueing.


Wait returns that child’s terminal Result. WaitAll returns one terminal outcome per requested child and MUST preserve child identity even when one or more children fail. WaitAny returns when the first requested child reaches a terminal state and identifies that child. Join operations MUST NOT flatten or discard per-child errors, blockers, logs, token usage, model provenance or tool records.


Identity and state


Every Subagent MUST expose SubagentID, ParentSubagentID?, ParentRequestID, RootRequestID, SessionID, EndpointID, Depth, State, CreatedAt, StartedAt?, FinishedAt?, Model and its effective tool/permission/budget configuration. IDs MUST be stable for the lifetime/history of that execution and MUST NOT be derived from display names, array position or queue position.


Subagent State MUST distinguish at least Created, Queued, Running, Waiting, Pausing, Paused, Completed, Failed, Blocked, Cancelled and TimedOut. Waiting means the Subagent is suspended awaiting dependencies/children and MUST NOT retain an execution slot that prevents those dependencies from running.


Scheduling and parallel execution


Ordinary requests on one endpoint remain serial by default as defined by the Runtime queue contract. Subagents do not silently change that rule. A parent waiting on a child that requires the same endpoint MUST yield its execution slot so the child can run; this is mandatory anti-deadlock behaviour.


Sibling Subagents assigned to different eligible endpoints MAY execute concurrently subject to resource, provider and configured concurrency limits. Siblings assigned to the same endpoint execute serially unless that endpoint explicitly advertises concurrent execution and the request enables the supported parallel mode.


Model = Auto and Endpoint = Auto permit the Runtime scheduler to select an eligible model/endpoint using declared capabilities, permission/privacy constraints and resource policy. An explicitly selected Model or Endpoint MUST NOT be silently replaced merely to increase parallelism; inability to satisfy the explicit selection returns a structured scheduling/capability failure.


MaxParallelChildren is a hard upper bound on concurrently Running children beneath the configured parent scope. Children above that limit remain Queued. Runtime-wide endpoint/resource limits MAY further reduce actual concurrency but MUST NOT increase it above the declared limit.


Context inheritance


Context inheritance is explicit. Supported policies are None, Inherit and Selected(...). Inherit snapshots the authorised parent context at spawn time; it does not create unsynchronised mutable shared conversation state. Selected(...) copies only the declared messages/context objects/references. None starts without parent conversational context except identity/control metadata required by Runtime.


A child Result becomes visible to the parent through an explicit join/result path or another explicitly authorised shared data object. Child completion MUST NOT silently rewrite earlier parent messages or a sibling’s context. Multiple children MUST NOT concurrently mutate the same session history without an explicit revision/conflict mechanism.

Give each worker a bounded objective, relevant context, ownership boundaries, constraints, dependencies, expected deliverables and acceptance tests. Coordinate shared files and interfaces; detect conflicting edits, duplicate work, stale instructions and incompatible outputs.
The supervising worker must inspect actual outputs and integration results rather than accepting self-reported success. Users can inspect, redirect or stop one worker without unnecessarily terminating the whole task. Keep concurrency, usage, spending limits and the responsible workers visible.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Descendant permissions, hard limits and hierarchical budgets

sources.quote:
A Subagent MUST NOT acquire more authority than its parent/caller. Effective child authority is the intersection of the caller’s current authority, the parent’s effective authority and the scopes requested for the child. The same narrowing rule applies to tools, filesystem/data scopes, external integrations, network access, credentials and action approvals.


Permissions = Inherit and Tools = Inherit copy only currently effective parent scopes. Expired/revoked grants are not inherited and no new approval is created by spawning a child. An action that requires approval in the parent context still requires approval when attempted by a child. Subagent creation MUST NOT provide privilege escalation or approval bypass.


Hierarchical budgets


Subagent budgets are hierarchical. Descendant consumption contributes to the ancestor/root aggregate for tokens, time, steps, tool calls and cost. A child MAY request stricter limits than its parent; it MUST NOT enlarge any hard parent/root limit. Parent and root budget exhaustion prevents further descendant work from starting and stops or blocks active descendants at safe boundaries according to the relevant resource type.


SubagentBudget MUST support MaxTokens, MaxTime, MaxSteps, MaxToolCalls and MaxCost where those quantities are enforceable. Runtime resource policy MAY additionally constrain CPU, GPU, RAM, VRAM and endpoint occupancy. Provider-unavailable cost/token telemetry MUST use the Runtime’s existing null/Na rules and MUST NOT be treated as zero consumption.


Actual descendant consumption MUST be attributed to both the child and its ancestor aggregates without double-counting the same invocation. If the system reserves budget before dispatch, reservation and settlement MUST be visible separately from actual settled usage.


Depth, child and concurrency limits


SubagentLimits MUST support MaxChildren, MaxParallelChildren and MaxDepth. MaxChildren counts direct children created by the configured execution scope. MaxDepth is measured from the root request, whose depth is 0; its direct Subagents are depth 1. Creating a child that would exceed a hard limit MUST fail before child execution begins.


The Runtime MUST also enforce implementation-wide safety ceilings even when the caller requests larger values. The effective limit is the minimum of caller/request limits, inherited parent limits and Runtime/provider limits. Limit failures return stable structured codes including MaxChildrenExceeded, MaxDepthExceeded and ConcurrencyLimitExceeded.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Child join/failure policy, pause/stop/restart propagation

sources.quote:
Parallel sibling execution MUST retain independent terminal outcomes. One child failure MUST NOT erase successful sibling results. The parent/join operation receives a structured collection containing, for every child, SubagentID, terminal State, Result?, Errors?, Blockers?, FinishReason and relevant usage/telemetry.


SubagentFailurePolicy MUST support at least Collect, FailFast, RequireAll and BestEffort. Collect waits for requested children and returns every outcome. FailFast requests cancellation of still-unfinished siblings after the first terminal failure/blocker while retaining already completed results. RequireAll treats any non-successful required child as a failed join. BestEffort permits the parent to continue with successful children while preserving explicit failed/blocked/cancelled outcomes.


Failure policy changes orchestration/join behaviour only; it MUST NOT suppress logs, errors, blockers or completed side effects. External actions already completed by a failed/cancelled child are not automatically rolled back unless the action itself defines rollback semantics.


Cancellation, pause and restart propagation


Stopping a root request MUST stop all unfinished dependent descendants. Stopping a Subagent MUST stop its unfinished descendants but MUST NOT automatically stop its parent or independent siblings; the parent receives the child’s Cancelled outcome and applies its configured failure policy.


Pausing a parent MUST prevent it from dispatching new child work. Running dependent children follow the parent’s explicit pause policy: PauseChildren requests safe-boundary pause, LetChildrenFinish permits already-running children to complete, and StopChildren cancels them. If no policy is supplied, PauseChildren is the default.


Restart creates a new attempt for the targeted Subagent using the specified/current authorised context and preserves the prior attempt in history. Restart MUST NOT replay already completed consequential tool/external actions automatically. Replacement/cancellation of an ancestor MUST invalidate stale descendant approvals and provisional output.

Subagent operations add stable structured failures including SubagentNotFound, MaxChildrenExceeded, MaxDepthExceeded, ConcurrencyLimitExceeded, BudgetExceeded, DependencyFailed, CheckpointUnavailable and RestoreConflict. These follow the Runtime error contract and MUST NOT rely on free-form string parsing.
