sources.quote:
Dulche Den MUST persist the execution-tree metadata required to inspect and recover Subagent work: stable identities, parent/child relationships, request/attempt revisions, effective configuration, states, checkpoints, results, blockers/errors, tool/action records and durable side-effect evidence. * Collect, FailFast, RequireAll and BestEffort preserve the documented per-child outcomes.
* Root/child stop and parent pause propagation follow the documented dependency semantics.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Request-aware Tool Registry and semantic feasibility

sources.quote:
Dulche MUST expose a canonical request-aware Tool Registry describing the tools, executable capabilities and usable resources that a model can employ to satisfy a request. The registry is broader than a literal list of function names: it includes first-party 9to1 app actions/APIs, Automations actions, Plugins, MCP tools, callable Agents, Skills that contribute executable workflows through authorised dependencies, Files/resource retrieval, image/audio/video generation capabilities, code/shell tools, web/network tools where permitted and other registered Dulche capabilities. Computer Use is represented only when it has been explicitly invoked under the Computer Use contract.
Every registry entry MUST use stable identity and structured metadata. At minimum it exposes ToolID/CapabilityID, source type and owner, version/revision, human-readable name, action IDs, semantic capability/intent tags, supported input/output types, parameter schemas, prerequisites, permission scopes, side-effect/risk classification, platform/scope constraints, availability/health and whether user approval or additional configuration is currently required. Display name and wording of an action MUST NOT be the sole mechanism used to decide what a tool can do.
Dulche MUST derive an EffectiveCapabilitySet for each request from the canonical registry. The effective set is filtered by the active user/profile, current app/Space/project, installed/enabled package state, app/API availability, explicit @ invocations, platform capability, privacy policy, administrator policy, current permissions/trust and any request-specific restrictions. Installed-but-unavailable, available-but-unapproved and immediately executable capabilities MUST remain distinguishable.
The active model/orchestrator MUST be given an inspectable, context-budget-aware representation of the EffectiveCapabilitySet. Dulche MAY provide a compact high-level catalogue initially and expose query/search APIs for deeper inspection so very large tool inventories do not consume the model's entire context. Capability discovery MUST nevertheless remain available throughout the request and MUST refresh when packages, permissions, target apps or connection state materially change.
Tool selection MUST be intent-based rather than exact-name-based. Dulche MUST translate the user's requested outcome into one or more semantic intents and compare those intents against tool capability metadata, schemas and declared examples/aliases. A tool does not need an action whose literal name matches the user's wording when its underlying capability can satisfy the requested effect.
For example, a request such as 'remind me tomorrow at 4 PM' MUST be resolvable to a time-triggered Automations operation even if no action is literally named CreateReminder. The semantic requirement is a durable time-based trigger that produces the requested notification/action. Likewise, 'create an image of ...' MUST resolve to an eligible image-generation capability such as the first-party image app/tool or an installed authorised image-generation Plugin, even if the tool's action is named Generate, Render, Imagine or another equivalent verb.
Capability resolution MUST support composition. If no single tool can fulfil the complete request but a sequence of authorised capabilities can, Dulche MUST be able to construct a typed ResolutionPlan whose steps pass structured outputs/references between tools. For example, a request to 'create an image and put it on the title slide' may resolve to image generation followed by Present insertion; a request to 'find the file and email it' may resolve to Files search followed by a Mail/Plugin send action, subject to normal permissions and approvals.
ResolutionPlan steps MUST identify the selected ToolID/CapabilityID, action, required arguments, expected outputs, dependencies, permission/approval state and why the step satisfies part of the user's intent. Capability resolution is planning, not execution: selecting a feasible tool MUST NOT bypass its normal permission, approval, confirmation, privacy, cost or side-effect rules.
Before a model states or implies that 9to1 cannot perform a requested digital action, it MUST first perform capability feasibility resolution against the current EffectiveCapabilitySet unless the impossibility is already established by a current authoritative hard constraint. The model MUST NOT answer 'I cannot directly create images', 'I cannot create reminders', 'I cannot access files' or equivalent merely because the base model itself lacks that native capability when Dulche exposes an authorised tool path that can perform it.
A capability that exists but is missing a prerequisite MUST be described as blocked/configuration-required rather than impossible. Examples include ApprovalRequired, PermissionDenied, AccountConnectionRequired, MissingRequiredInput, AppUnavailable, ProviderUnavailable, CapabilityDisabledByPolicy and UnsupportedOnCurrentPlatform. When the missing prerequisite can be resolved within the current request and permission bounds, Dulche SHOULD resolve it or ask only for the specific user decision/input required and then continue.
If several feasible tools can perform the same intent, Dulche MUST select according to explicit user invocation/instruction first, then applicable app ownership/canonical-data rules, privacy/locality policy, capability fitness, permissions, reliability and configured user preferences. Cost/latency MAY participate where policy allows. Dulche MUST NOT choose an unrelated or lower-fidelity tool merely because its action name more closely resembles the user's wording.
Explicit @ invocation remains authoritative. An @Plugin, @App, @Agent, @Skill or other invocation narrows or prioritises the capability source according to that invocation's contract. However, ordinary natural-language requests do NOT require the user to know or name the underlying tool. 'Create a presentation', 'set a reminder', 'generate an image' and similar outcome requests MUST be sufficient for Dulche to discover and use the appropriate capability when one is available.
Skills, Agents and Files participate according to their real semantics rather than being falsely treated as identical callable functions. A Skill may contribute instructions/workflow/tool dependencies; an Agent may be invoked as a delegated execution capability; a File/resource may provide required input/context; an App/Plugin/MCP/native action may perform the mutation. The resolver MUST be able to combine these heterogeneous entries into one plan while preserving their distinct identities, permissions and audit records.
Dulche MUST expose canonical discovery operations equivalent to Dulche.Tool.List(context?), Dulche.Tool.Search(intent, context?), Dulche.Tool.Get(toolID), Dulche.Tool.Resolve(intent, context?) and Dulche.Tool.ExplainResolution(resolutionID). Resolve MUST return either one or more ranked feasible ResolutionPlans or a structured no-feasible-path result containing the evaluated hard constraints and missing prerequisites. Search/Resolve MUST use semantic capability metadata in addition to lexical names.
The Runtime MUST cache capability metadata efficiently but MUST version/invalidate the cache when relevant package versions, app capabilities, connection state, permissions, policy or provider health change. A model MUST NOT continue relying on a stale 'tool unavailable' conclusion after the capability registry has materially changed during the request.
A tool-result or retrieved document MUST NOT be able to self-register new authority merely by claiming that another tool exists or should be allowed. Registry membership and permissions come from trusted Dulche/Home registration, package manifests, app capability contracts and current policy. Semantic discovery MUST therefore improve capability use without creating a prompt-injection route to invented tools or escalated permissions.
Failure to resolve a tool path MUST be truthful and inspectable. Dulche MUST distinguish NoMatchingCapability from MatchingCapabilityUnavailable, MissingPrerequisite, PermissionBlocked and PolicyBlocked. When no feasible path exists, the model MAY explain the limitation, but it MUST NOT fabricate a tool or claim to have performed the action. The Resolution attempt and selected/no-selected candidates MUST be visible in FullLog/Action Graph at an appropriate level of detail.
Acceptance coverage MUST verify at minimum that: a reminder request resolves to an Automations time-based workflow without requiring the phrase 'automation'; an image-generation request invokes an eligible image capability rather than returning a false inability statement; a presentation request can resolve to Present from another app; a multi-tool request produces a dependency-ordered ResolutionPlan; explicit @ invocation overrides automatic source choice; permission/configuration blockers are distinguished from true impossibility; Computer Use does not appear unless explicitly invoked; and removal/disablement of the only matching capability causes a structured no-feasible-path result rather than a fabricated success.

requirements.requirement: P1 — Dulche Result identity, logs, thinking and metric availability

sources.quote:
Return Result using the exact field names below. The question mark denotes optional content, not part of the field name. Empty metrics return null. Provider-unavailable metrics return Na, serialised as the exact JSON string "Na" and exposed by typed bindings as an unavailable sentinel. A measured zero remains 0. This applies to all metrics, including those not originally marked optional and nested model metrics.


Use value/null/Na-capable types and separate availability/provenance metadata for pending, disabled/redacted, measured, estimated and provider-unavailable values. Never substitute zero or an invented value for unavailable data. Required identity/status and the Runtime event-log container remain present. Collections with no applicable entries may be null; numeric counts may be a measured zero. A complete aggregate cannot silently ignore unavailable contributions.


Response content and identity
Text: the actual user-facing response, separate from tool arguments and undisclosed provider internals. No text may have been produced for a blocked, cancelled or non-text-only response.


Thinking: the thinking log actually exposed and permitted by the model/provider. Label traces and summaries distinctly; never present a summary as the complete internal thinking or reconstruct undisclosed reasoning. Empty content is null; provider-unavailable thinking is Na.


Tools?: identities of the distinct tools actually used, with links to invocations. Tools offered but not called are not counted as used.


Sources?: sources retrieved, supplied or cited, with provenance and relevant response-span references. Distinguish retrieved evidence from unverified model-generated citations.


GeneratedUI?: structured, versioned UI data, separate from Text and rendered only through an explicit CUI integration.


Models: models actually used, including agent/subtask models, in first-use order and deduplicated by artifact/provider revision. Preserve roles, call counts, endpoints and invocation records. Models[i].Parameters exposes the individual parameter metric.


Also return RequestID, SessionID, Endpoint, Status, FinishReason, request revision and attempt identity. FinishReason distinguishes Completed, Cancelled, Replaced, Blocked, Error, OutputLimit and Refused. Paused is a non-terminal state, not successful completion. Preserve the original provider finish reason separately.


Earlier shorthand fields are compatibility views: Reasoning maps to Thinking; Model identifies the primary responding model; TokenUsage groups the token metrics; Error is the primary error from Errors. ToolCalls contains individual invocations, while Tools is their tool-identity summary. Endpoint identifies the primary request endpoint; additional endpoints remain in Models and logs.

AuditLog?: timestamped reads, writes and other actions, with actor, request/attempt, target, permission/approval, start/end, outcome and side effects. ToolLog?: every tool invocation with ID, tool/version, timestamps, safe arguments/results, outcome and correlation IDs. Tools is the summary; ToolLog is the invocation history.


FullLog: the continuous ordered collection of Runtime-observed actions, model calls, available thinking/summary events, tools, queue events, pauses, replacements, retries, approvals, results, blockers and errors. Include UTC timestamps, per-request sequence numbers and causal parent IDs. Do not fabricate exact global ordering for concurrent work. Stream/paginate large logs without losing continuity. Undisclosed provider internals are not promised; sensitive payloads are redacted/permission-filtered with omissions recorded.


Blockers?: structured reasons work cannot complete, with affected scope, evidence, attempted recovery, whether human input is needed, next action and retryability. Errors?: hard model/provider/Runtime/tool failures with stable code, message, component, timestamp, request identity and safe details. A blocker need not be a crash; cancellation need not be a hard error. Keep recoverable retries/warnings in logs.


Use structured results for ModelNotFound, MissingPrompt, EndpointNotFound, PortInUse, InvalidArgument, OutOfMemory, ContextExceeded, ProviderUnavailable, AuthenticationFailed, PermissionDenied, UnsupportedCapability, ToolFailed, RequestNotFound, InvalidState, QueueFull, Conflict and ModelLoadFailed. Preserve "model not found" as the friendly message for resolution failure. Expected operational failures must not depend on string parsing or unhandled exceptions.
Round-trip null for empty metrics and Na for provider-unavailable metrics, serialised as "Na"; measured zero stays 0. Permission-filter search/index results and include revision/provenance.

requirements.requirement: P1 — Timing, token attribution, model placement and storage resources

sources.quote:
TimeElapsed: wall-clock seconds from acceptance to terminal result, including queueing/pauses; live snapshots measure through the snapshot time. Expose queue, pause and execution duration separately.


TimeThinking?: attributable thinking duration. TimeAgentic?: duration of agent/tool work. TimeResponding: duration of generating the actual response. Use backend events or observed spans, not an assumption that all pre-first-token delay is thinking. Parallel and nested spans may overlap, so phase totals need not sum to TimeElapsed; report timing basis and estimate status.


InputTokens: input processed by all included model invocations. OutputTokens: output generated by those invocations, including reported non-visible reasoning/tool output where applicable. TotalTokens equals InputTokens plus OutputTokens when both are known. Preserve provider tokenisation, cached-token details, modality usage and billing data per invocation.


ResponseTokens: output tokens attributable to the user-facing response. AgenticTokens?: output tokens attributed to agent orchestration/tool-call work. ThinkingTokens?: backend/provider-reported thinking tokens. These are labelled subsets of OutputTokens, not extra quantities to add to it. Subsets can overlap, such as thinking within an agent step; retain attribution rather than inventing a mutually exclusive split.


Aggregate actual invocations, including retries, within an explicit request/attempt/task scope. Do not double-count a child invocation through both parent and child totals. If a contributing provider withholds a required metric, the complete aggregate is Na; return a separate known subtotal and coverage when useful. Supported metrics with no value yet are null.

Parameters: architectural parameter totals across distinct model revisions actually used, counted once per model rather than once per prompt/instance. This is not a claim that several models behave like one larger model. Report per-model total and active MoE parameter counts separately when known, and label declared architectural active counts versus observed routing.


Location: structured model-weight placement with a readable form such as "9.3% GPU | 90.7% RAM". This is residency, not utilisation. Include device IDs, measurement time/window, quantity basis, sampling method and any other/unknown location. Do not confuse parameter share with byte share, or include KV cache/activations as model weights. Shared/unified memory must not be double-counted.


MoEs expose separate Active and Total placement views. State the denominator: an active-set distribution normalises to the active set; active weights expressed as a share of all parameters must be labelled accordingly. Keep underlying quantities. A display such as "Active: 19.9% GPU | 20.1% RAM; Total: 6% GPU | 94% RAM" needs an explicit basis and remaining share; do not silently normalise or fabricate missing placement. Hidden provider placement is Na.


Storage: disk bytes occupied by response-associated model artifacts, not VRAM/RAM, token usage or cumulative download traffic. Deduplicate shared artifacts within each physical storage location and show local/device/remote breakdowns. Unknown remote storage makes the complete total Na, while a known local subtotal may be shown. Distinguish persistent versus temporary artifacts.

Expose runtime/API/schema versions, states, queues, tokens/context, memory/storage, rate-limit status, time to first output, generation throughput and trace IDs through permission-filtered diagnostics. Use Na for unavailable telemetry, null for empty telemetry and labels for estimates. Publish SDK/adapter conformance tests and compatibility negotiation.


Acceptance covers serial A/B queueing, streaming/non-streaming parity, every response control, queued/running/paused/completed replacement, null/Na/zero, withheld provider metrics/thinking, token aggregation, MoE denominators, scoped broadcasts, context isolation, unsupported exact resume, tool retry/cancellation, generated-UI fallback, provider failure, memory pressure and recovery.

sources.quote: Pass 1 includes ALL requirements of the former Pass 4: Lunar Eclipse, including its complete LE-01–LE-15 contracts, product descriptions, reference material, tests and applicable platform obligations. Those requirements are incorporated into Pass 1 in full and retained at their existing document location under “Pass 1 incorporated requirements: Lunar Eclipse (LE-01–LE-15)”. They are not a separate later pass or deferred scope. Existing LE identifiers and precise supersessions remain valid; references within that section to “this pass” mean the incorporated Lunar Eclipse requirements of Pass 1. Pass 2 Terra-form and Pass 3 Sol Happy remain intact; unrelated post-release scope is not added. Pass membership does not change technical ownership: Team A owns native/shared work, Team B browser work and Team C hosted services and global integration.

Pass 4 MUST add a Dulche-owned inference-runtime abstraction so model definitions and higher-level Dulche features do not depend directly on one execution engine. llama.cpp remains the broad/default local backend. Dulche MUST also include an upstream-trackable Strata fork as a specialised backend for model architectures where Strata is supported and materially better suited.


Runtime abstraction and dispatcher
Dulche MUST expose one stable internal runtime contract for model loading, prompt/prefill, decode, context/KV handling, multimodal inputs where supported, cancellation, streaming, usage/telemetry, errors and shutdown. Engine-specific behaviour belongs behind adapters. Agents, Spaces, Plugins, Skills and other Dulche callers MUST target the Dulche runtime contract rather than importing llama.cpp- or Strata-specific APIs.


A Runtime Dispatcher MUST select the effective inference engine per model. Selection MUST be capability-based rather than a simple dense-versus-MoE rule. The compatibility registry MUST be able to consider model architecture/family, file/weight format, quantisation, required runtime features, OS, available VRAM, system RAM, CPU capabilities and any other hard backend requirement. A model manifest MAY declare a preferred engine and fallback engines, but the manifest MUST NOT make the model permanently dependent on one backend.


Automatic selection
Automatic selection is the default. Dulche MUST first remove incompatible engines, then choose between compatible engines using declared capability fit and locally measured performance where useful. Calibration MAY benchmark compatible engines for a model/quantisation/hardware fingerprint and cache the result so repeated launches do not re-run expensive benchmarks. Prefill and decode MUST be measured separately where they have materially different performance characteristics.


Automatic selection MUST NOT enable quality-reducing or behaviour-changing experimental flags merely to win a performance comparison. Runtime choice MUST remain inspectable through diagnostics/logging, including the selected engine and the reason it was selected.

Dulche MUST carry a maintained Strata fork rather than treating a separately installed Strata application as a required user dependency. The fork MUST preserve applicable upstream and third-party licence notices, keep model-weight licences separate, and remain intentionally close enough to upstream that security, correctness and performance improvements can be reviewed and merged without repeatedly re-forking the project.


The Dulche Strata adapter MUST expose Strata through the same Dulche runtime contract used by llama.cpp. Strata-specific optimisations such as expert caching/residency, concurrent CPU/GPU expert execution, specialised prefill, MTP/speculative execution and model-specific memory placement MAY be used when supported, but they MUST remain implementation details behind the common runtime boundary.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Context compaction and bounded summarisation preserve obligations

sources.quote:
Context compaction is a first-class Dulche Runtime capability, not an app-specific prompt trick. Dulche MUST track the effective context budget for every model invocation and MAY initiate automatic compaction before hard exhaustion using model/provider-specific safety margins. Apps and Agents consume the same canonical compacted session state rather than implementing incompatible private compaction.
Compaction MUST preserve semantic obligations required to continue the task: current user instructions and constraints, active permissions/trust decisions, CompletionContract, outstanding tasks and blockers, accepted decisions, stable object/file/artifact IDs, current revisions, completed consequential actions, verification evidence, relevant source provenance and any exact values whose precision is required. Redundant conversational phrasing, duplicated status chatter and obsolete intermediate reasoning MAY be reduced.
Compaction MUST be non-destructive to durable history. The original authorised conversation, tool records and artifacts remain in Den according to retention policy; the compacted context is a derived execution view with provenance back to source message/event ranges. A model MUST NOT be told that omitted content never existed merely because it is outside the active compacted view.
If ordinary compaction cannot create enough safe context without materially losing required information or required media fidelity, Dulche MUST transition to Context Summarisation rather than silently dropping required content or returning ContextExceeded immediately. Typical triggers include a conversation dominated by images/media that cannot be reduced further without unacceptable information loss, unusually dense tool history, or a model whose effective context limit is smaller than the preserved minimum working set.
Context Summarisation is a distinct Dulche job. A summariser model reads the retained conversation/history section by section using bounded windows so the summariser's own context cannot overflow. Each section produces a structured intermediate summary containing obligations, facts, decisions, identifiers, artifacts/references, completed actions, unresolved work/blockers, provenance and continuity notes. Dulche then performs one or more bounded merge passes until a final execution summary fits the target context budget.
Section boundaries MUST be deterministic and provenance-preserving. A merge MUST NOT discard a requirement merely because it appears only once. Conflicting instructions or facts MUST remain represented as a conflict with source references instead of being flattened into an invented resolution. Exact code, identifiers, numeric values, legal/technical constraints or other precision-sensitive content that cannot be safely paraphrased MUST remain as pinned excerpts or stable references rather than approximate prose.
Images, audio, video and other large artifacts SHOULD remain out-of-band as stable artifact references wherever the target model can retrieve them on demand. Context Summarisation MAY summarise authorised derived observations/metadata, but MUST NOT claim that visual or media detail was preserved if the summariser could not inspect it. Required uninspectable media remains a blocker or retained reference, not fabricated text.
A local summariser model MAY be used automatically when an eligible local model is available under the configured routing/policy. requirements.requirement: P0 — Den portable schema, cross-harness state and safe import

sources.quote:
Dulche Den is Dulche's persistent, cross-harness storage standard. It allows Dulche state to remain available across compatible apps and harnesses rather than being tied to one running endpoint or one application session.


Model catalogue
A user's Den can maintain their model catalogue using stable model IDs alongside user-facing names. IDs provide unambiguous model references; names are intended for human-facing use and may be duplicated, which is why name lookup returns a list rather than assuming a single match.


Cross-app state
Den is also intended to provide persistent storage for cross-app context, agents and related Dulche state so compatible 9to1 surfaces can share the same underlying information instead of maintaining isolated copies.


Storage structure and portability
Den is a directory-based persistent store with a versioned den.json manifest, structured records, a transaction journal and separately stored or referenced large objects. Portable records use UTF-8 JSON; local databases and indexes may accelerate access but must not be the only readable copy or create an incompatible private format. Exports contain authorised records and explicitly selected attachments. Reference model weights and external Files documents by identity/content hash rather than copying them by default. No special bundle extension is mandated.


The manifest identifies DenID, FormatVersion, SchemaVersion, minimum reader/writer versions, namespaces, storage locations and required capabilities. Validate manifests, paths, sizes and hashes before import. Importing never executes code or automatically enables agents, tools, connections or permissions.


Identity, namespaces and model records
Every model, agent, conversation, context object, workflow and request has a stable ID independent of name/path. Separate personal, team, organisation and app namespaces; device paths and hardware settings stay device-local. Shared namespaces are opt-in.


Model records contain logical ID, display name, aliases, provider/source, immutable revision/artifact hash, family, format, quantisation, modalities/capabilities, context/output limits, ordered reasoning levels, configuration overrides, installation references, timestamps, provenance and replacement history. Parameters, active MoE parameters, storage and hardware metrics use Runtime's availability rules. Local paths are not portable identities.


ID lookup is unambiguous in its namespace. Name/property lookup returns all matches, never silently chooses a duplicate. Aliases are explicit namespace-scoped references. Model replacement may retain logical ID/name but records changed artifact/provider identity, retained/reset settings and rollback history.


Sessions, context and checkpoints
Den persists messages/revisions, authorised context, agent definitions, requests/results, tool records, approvals and checkpoints as distinct record types. Runtime executes work; Den stores information needed to inspect or resume it.


Portability covers supported messages, context, configuration, definitions and history, not arbitrary backend caches, GPU state or undisclosed internal model state. Checkpoints declare backend/model compatibility. Distinguish a continuation attempt from exact resumption and never automatically repeat completed external actions.


Context records identify source, owning app, timestamps, author/inference provenance, access scope and retention. Distinguish user-authored, imported and inferred context. Sharing a conversation does not automatically share its referenced sources, secrets, attachments or private inferences.

Publish versioned schemas, examples and conformance tests. Compatible writers preserve unknown optional fields; unknown security-critical fields or required capabilities block unsafe writes. Validate, back up and transactionally migrate schemas. Unsupported newer versions may open read-only when safe, never discard fields to force a downgrade.


Round-trip null for empty metrics and Na for provider-unavailable metrics, serialised as "Na"; measured zero stays 0. Permission-filter search/index results and include revision/provenance.


Supporting APIs and acceptance
Preserve Dulche.Den.GetModelByID(id) and Dulche.Den.ListModelsByName(name). Add compatible create/open, scoped search, revision-checked update, export/import, sync, restore and purge APIs with documented signatures and failures.


Acceptance covers cross-harness round-tripping, duplicate names, concurrent edits, offline conflicts, crash recovery, revocation, safe import, secret-free export, model replacement/rollback, retention/restore and migrations without data loss.

requirements.requirement: P1 — Persistent Memory frequencies, scope and temporary-chat suppression

sources.quote:
Persistent Memory is a core Dulche Den subsystem for durable cross-session information about the user, recurring entities, preferences, decisions, projects and other scoped context that Dulche should be able to retrieve in future conversations or authorised surfaces. It is separate from Background Learning.
Memory is not one opaque prompt file. A persistent MemoryEntry should carry stable identity, content or structured value, subject/entity, memory type/category, scope, source/provenance, confidence where applicable, created/updated state, supersession/correction relationships, retention state and user-edited/locked state where supported.
Scopes
Memory can be scoped so unrelated Agents/apps do not receive unnecessary context. Supported scopes should include global/user memory plus narrower project, Agent, app/surface or other explicit contexts where appropriate. Retrieval MUST respect both scope and permission.
Creation and retrieval
Dulche may create or update memories from eligible conversations/context according to the user's Memory Frequency and memory policy. Retrieval is relevance-based: only memories useful to the active request/context should be injected, rather than the complete memory store.
Explicit user corrections supersede contradictory earlier memories. Den MUST retain enough provenance/revision information to distinguish an explicit user statement from an inference and to avoid repeatedly resurfacing a memory that has been corrected, superseded or deleted.
Memory Frequency
Settings MUST expose a Memory Frequency preference with exactly four user-facing levels: Never, Sometimes, Often and Always. The selected level controls how readily Dulche autonomously creates, reinforces or updates Persistent Memory from eligible non-temporary interactions.
* Never: Dulche MUST NOT autonomously create, reinforce or update Persistent Memory from ordinary interactions. Direct user-invoked memory-management actions are separate explicit operations.
* Sometimes: use a conservative threshold and retain only clearly durable, repeatedly useful or high-value information.
* Often: use a lower threshold and remember useful preferences, decisions, entities and ongoing context more readily when they are likely to help future responses.
* Always: evaluate every eligible interaction for durable memory and normally retain information that satisfies the memory policy, while still deduplicating noise, respecting scope/retention rules and avoiding ineligible information.
Changing Memory Frequency affects future autonomous memory behaviour; it MUST NOT silently delete existing memories. The setting is independent of Background Learning.
Temporary chats in Spaces
Spaces can provide Temporary Chats. Persistent Memory creation is disabled inside a Temporary Chat regardless of the user's Memory Frequency. While a chat is temporary, Dulche MUST NOT autonomously create, update, reinforce, merge or promote Persistent Memory from that conversation.
Any explicit action that would save new Persistent Memory from a Temporary Chat must be unavailable or clearly report that memory creation is disabled for temporary chats. Temporary-chat memory-write suppression MUST NOT be bypassed by an Agent, plugin, Skill, tool or Background Learning pipeline.
This rule governs memory creation/writes. Whether existing authorised memories are retrieved into a temporary chat is a separate context/privacy policy and MUST NOT be inferred from the memory-write prohibition.
Management and lifecycle
Users must be able to inspect, search, edit/correct, supersede and delete persistent memories through the appropriate settings/Den surfaces. Deletion and retention use Den's normal lifecycle, sync and purge contracts. Memory export/import must preserve scopes, provenance and deletion/supersession semantics rather than flattening entries into plain prose.
Persistent Memory acceptance requirements
* Persistent Memory exists as a distinct Den record system and is not substituted by Background Learning, session context or Agent-only memory.
* Memory retrieval is relevance-, scope- and permission-aware.
* Never/Sometimes/Often/Always control autonomous memory creation/reinforcement with the semantics above.
* Temporary Chats in Spaces cannot create, update or reinforce Persistent Memory regardless of frequency or calling surface.
* Corrections/supersession are durable and user-manageable, and explicit user statements remain distinguishable from inference.

requirements.requirement: P1 — Independent opt-in Background Learning and Knowledge Banks

sources.quote:
Background Learning is an explicitly opt-in Dulche personalisation subsystem. It is separate from Persistent Memory. Enabling Background Learning allows Dulche to learn useful patterns, interests and reusable knowledge from eligible 9to1 activity over time; it does not itself enable or disable Persistent Memory and it does not imply continuous fine-tuning of the underlying base model.
Eligible learning classes
Background Learning can maintain three broad classes of learned information:
* 9to1 usage and project context: which authorised surfaces the user uses most, recurring workflows, recently or frequently active projects, apps commonly used together, important project terminology/entities and other usage patterns that improve contextual relevance.
* Interests and topic Knowledge Banks: recurring subjects the user appears to care about, together with reusable factual/reference material that can improve later answers and remain available offline. For example, repeated questions about cars may lead to an Interest record for cars and a local Cars Knowledge Bank containing useful terminology, concepts and sourced reference material.
* Other relevant personalisation information: additional permitted information that materially improves responses, such as preferred terminology, recurring goals, explanation preferences, established project conventions, frequently used tools, entity relationships and corrections that should influence future response behaviour.
Usage and project learning
The usage-learning layer SHOULD retain useful semantic state rather than an indiscriminate permanent clickstream. For example, it may learn that Dev and Stack are frequently used for a particular project or that a project is currently active. Raw activity used to derive these signals should be retained only to the extent required by the configured retention/privacy model.
Learned project context can help Dulche resolve ambiguous references, rank context candidates, suggest likely relevant surfaces and prepare authorised Agents with useful project context. It MUST remain scope-aware: project-specific learning does not automatically become unrelated global context.
Interest Knowledge Banks
Background Learning can create and maintain topic-specific KnowledgeBank entities. A KnowledgeBank can contain a stable ID, topic/title, entries, source/provenance metadata, confidence, freshness, creation/update state, storage/sync policy and enabled/disabled state. Knowledge Banks may be created automatically from recurring interests or explicitly managed by the user.
Knowledge Bank entries may include reusable summaries, terminology, relationships, reference facts and other material previously obtained from authorised local sources, user interactions or trusted retrieval. Factual entries MUST retain enough provenance/freshness information for Dulche to distinguish durable knowledge from information that may need refreshing.
Knowledge Banks are not the same as Persistent Memory. For example, 'the user is interested in cars' is personalisation/user context; a structured offline bank explaining engines, EV charging and vehicle terminology is subject knowledge. Dulche may use both when relevant, but they remain separately inspectable and manageable.
Structured learned state
Background Learning MUST store structured learned records rather than relying on one opaque free-form profile. Records should carry stable identity, category/type, subject/entity, learned value, provenance, confidence, creation/update state, last reinforcement/use where useful, freshness/expiry semantics and user-edited/locked state where applicable.
Explicit user corrections outrank contradictory inferred learning. If a user corrects an inferred preference, project status or interest, the system MUST revise/supersede the stale inference instead of allowing both to compete indefinitely as equally valid facts.
Selective retrieval
The complete learning store MUST NOT be injected into every request. Dulche must retrieve only learning context relevant to the active request, Agent, app and permission scope. Retrieval should use current entities/topics/project context to select the smallest useful set of records and Knowledge Bank material.
Privacy and cloud boundaries
Background Learning data is private by default and exists to personalise the user's 9to1 AI experience. It MUST NOT be sold, used to build advertising profiles or indiscriminately uploaded to third parties. Enabling Background Learning does not itself grant permission to transmit learned information to a cloud model/provider.
If a Dulche request uses a remote/cloud provider, disclosure of any learned context remains subject to the normal provider, privacy, permission and data-minimisation rules for that request. The implementation MUST distinguish permission to learn/store information from permission to disclose that information externally.
Any optional cross-device synchronisation of Background Learning state must be user-controlled and protected by the applicable authenticated/encrypted 9to1 sync/storage architecture. The feature MUST remain useful locally and must not require insecure cloud upload merely to personalise responses.
User controls
Users must be able to enable/disable Background Learning, pause new learning, inspect learned information, inspect and manage topic Knowledge Banks, correct inaccurate learning, delete individual learned records or a complete topic bank, clear learned categories and configure which apps/projects/categories may contribute where supported. Disabling learning stops creation/reinforcement of new learned state but MUST NOT silently delete existing Persistent Memory or unrelated user data.
Relationship to Persistent Memory
Persistent Memory and Background Learning are independent. Persistent Memory stores durable cross-session memories under the Memory policy; Background Learning is the opt-in process that derives usage patterns, interests, Knowledge Banks and other personalisation state. Neither feature may silently enable, disable, clear or substitute for the other.
Background Learning may identify information that would be useful as a durable memory, but any conversion into Persistent Memory must use the Memory subsystem and preserve that the source was an inference rather than an explicit user statement. Explicit Memory corrections remain authoritative over contradictory Background Learning inferences.
Background Learning acceptance requirements
* Background Learning is off until the user opts in and remains independently configurable from Persistent Memory.
* Eligible 9to1 usage/project patterns, interests/Knowledge Banks and other useful personalisation information can be learned as structured, inspectable state.
* Topic Knowledge Banks can provide relevant offline reference material and retain provenance/freshness sufficient to avoid presenting stale inferred facts as timeless truth.
* Only relevant learning context is retrieved for a request; the full learning store is not injected indiscriminately.
* Learned data is not sold, used for advertising profiles or uploaded to cloud providers merely because learning is enabled.
* Users can inspect, correct, scope and delete learning independently of Persistent Memory.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Generative UI validated state/action trust and canonical artifacts

sources.quote: GeneratedUI is returned as data. A CUI developer explicitly implements <GenerativeContainer> and advertises supported schemas/components/actions. Without it, retain a usable text/data fallback rather than assume rendering support. Validate components, properties, limits, references and action bindings; model output never becomes trusted executable application code. UI actions use authorised typed tools tied to the request/revision. Invalid generated UI is isolated/logged without crashing the app or losing Text.

Generative UI is a Dulche capability that allows a model or Agent to return arbitrary structured user interfaces when an interface is more useful than prose. Generated interfaces may be visual, interactive and stateful, but MUST be expressed through a validated declarative Generative UI schema and MUST NOT execute arbitrary model-generated application code.
Rendering and trust boundary
CUI is the rendering layer for Generative UI. Generated surfaces render inside a CUI <GenerativeContainer> or equivalent trusted host component using approved CUI primitives, design tokens, theming, layout, accessibility and interaction behaviour. Any authorised 9to1 app may host a GenerativeContainer without implementing its own incompatible renderer.
Dulche may choose the structure and composition of the interface, including novel layouts, but the model output is data/schema rather than executable JavaScript, Python, shell commands, native binaries or arbitrary application code. The Generative UI runtime validates schema version, component types, properties, state bindings, declared actions and capability references before rendering.

When no template fully fits the task, Dulche can compose a custom surface from approved lower-level primitives. The supported primitive set should include, where appropriate, text/heading blocks, icons or generated illustrations, cards, badges/tags, buttons, inputs, dropdowns, toggles, sliders, chips, lists, tables, grids, tabs, accordions, progress indicators, layout containers, drag containers, drop zones, connectors/relationships, semantic-object views and other safe CUI primitives.
The primitive library is extensible through versioned framework/extension contracts. Unsupported component types MUST be rejected or downgraded safely; a model cannot create a new privileged executable component merely by naming it in the schema.
State and interaction
Generated surfaces may maintain bounded typed state. Supported interactions can include selecting options, sorting/filtering, expanding/collapsing content, progressing through steps, editing fields, revealing hints/answers, checking responses, reordering items, dragging supported objects between declared drop zones, switching views and updating selected data.
State mutations are handled by the Generative UI runtime or by declared typed actions. Interaction support does not grant the model arbitrary code execution or unrestricted access to the host application's process.
Progressive conversational evolution
A generated surface is a first-class conversation artifact and may evolve across turns. Dulche should be able to patch or transform an existing surface instead of rebuilding unrelated output from scratch. Examples include turning a static explanation into an interactive exercise, adding another column to a table, converting notes into flashcards, adding filters, changing a card grid into a comparison view or preserving quiz progress while adding new questions.
Updates must address stable SurfaceID/component/state identities or equivalent schema identities so user interaction state is retained wherever the requested transformation allows it. Partial regeneration is preferred when only part of a surface changes.
Typed actions and side effects
Generated controls bind to declared typed actions rather than arbitrary executable handlers. An action definition includes stable identity, expected input schema, allowed state mutation or API binding, required capability/permission and result/error contract.
Pure presentation and local interaction may execute inside the Generative UI runtime without external side effects. Actions that invoke 9to1 APIs, tools or external services remain subject to the same permission, confirmation, auditing and consequence rules as the underlying capability. Generative UI MUST NOT be a path around security prompts or tool permissions.
Data binding and semantic objects
Generative UI can bind to authorised structured data and canonical 9to1 entities instead of flattening everything into prompt text. Examples include Data ranges, Planner tasks, Maps Places/Routes, Board items, Write selections/documents, search results, translation sets, code diffs or Dulche Action Graph state.
Bindings retain source identity and permissions. A rendered card or table row that represents a canonical object should reference that object rather than silently creating a disconnected copy unless the user explicitly asks for a snapshot.
Ephemeral and saved artifacts
A generated surface may remain ephemeral to the current response/session or be promoted through an explicit supported conversion/save path. Examples include saving generated flashcards as a study resource, converting a generated task board into a Board, inserting a generated table into Write/Data or saving a generated route through Maps. Promotion uses the destination app's canonical API and permissions.
Third-party visual examples and assets
Generative UI may reproduce the functional idea or spatial structure needed to explain a third-party product/game without copying proprietary artwork merely to imitate the source. Where licensed/authorised assets are not available, it should use generic, stylised, text-labelled or newly generated representations sufficient to communicate the concept.
Example: if the user asks how an item is crafted in Minecraft, Dulche may create a visual 3x3 crafting-grid representation using generic/stylised ingredient tokens and an output slot rather than copied official item textures or proprietary interface artwork. In later turns the same surface may be made interactive using approved drag/drop primitives so the user can move ingredient tokens, receive validation, request hints or turn the recipe into a quiz.
Accessibility and visual consistency
Generated UI MUST inherit the host CUI theme/design system and remain accessible. The runtime should enforce semantic roles, labels, focusability/order, keyboard operation, screen-reader information, non-colour-only meaning and accessible alternatives for interactions such as drag/drop wherever the component library supports them.
Failure and fallback
Invalid, unsupported or unsafe generated schemas MUST fail closed without executing arbitrary content. Dulche may repair/regenerate the affected surface or fall back to a non-interactive/native representation while preserving the user-visible answer where possible.
Result contract and acceptance
Result.GeneratedUI contains the generated UI payload when present and returns null when no generated interface is produced. The payload must identify schema version, surface identity, component tree, declared state/bindings and declared actions/capabilities required to reproduce the surface safely.
* Dulche can create arbitrary useful UI structures without arbitrary code execution.
* Built-in templates and lower-level CUI primitives can be combined and extended within the declarative schema.
* Generated surfaces support safe stateful interaction and can evolve across conversation turns without unnecessarily discarding user state.
* All external side effects route through typed permission-aware actions.
* Structured 9to1 data can be bound by canonical identity, and generated artifacts can be promoted through destination-app APIs.
* Generated UI follows CUI theming/accessibility and safely handles invalid schemas or unavailable components.

This switcher is a platform-wide interaction contract used consistently by Write, Present, Boards, Files, Canvas, Data, Mail, Planner and every other surface that hosts the shared bar.


In Read-only mode, Dulche MAY read, search, compare, reason over, summarise, explain and navigate the full authorised semantic surface, including off-screen content that the owning app exposes. It MAY generate proposed changes in conversation, but MUST NOT mutate the owning artifact, structure or app state. Read-only access does not imply permission to inspect data outside the caller's normal authorisation boundary.


In Write mode, Dulche receives the same semantic read context plus the owning app's permitted typed mutation actions. Write mode is capability to request/perform edits, not permission to bypass app state, trust, confirmation, review, external-side-effect or security rules. Mutations MUST use stable semantic identities such as ArtifactID, PageID, SectionID, ObjectID, row/range/entity IDs or equivalent domain identifiers and the owning app's normal revision/conflict semantics.


The AI-bar mode is separate from the host app's own Edit/View/Suggest/Locked/Unlocked or equivalent state. For example, an AI bar in Write mode does not silently bypass a Board that is currently in View mode, and a Write document in Suggest mode represents permitted AI edits as suggestions rather than accepted direct edits. Host-surface rules may narrow the effective mutation set further.


Apps MUST provide a permission-filtered semantic context snapshot including the active artifact/page/entity, current selection, relevant stable object IDs, structure necessary to understand the task, current revision/state and supported typed actions. The bar MUST prefer this semantic context over screenshot/OCR/pixel interpretation and MUST NOT substitute raw mouse/keyboard/desktop automation when typed context/actions exist.


The AI bar MUST remain visually separate from document/page content and MUST NOT change the underlying artifact layout merely by being shown. It MAY collapse to a compact state but MUST remain directly reachable without navigating to a separate AI page. Read/Write mode changes the AI's effective capability only; it does not create a second copy of the current artifact.


Surface-specific mutation protections MAY be stricter than the shared Write-mode baseline and cannot be weakened by AI mode or trust state. Data is the mandatory example: every AI-requested Data mutation requires explicit approval for that specific action even while the bar is in Write mode. When the target is a live database, Data MUST additionally show a meaningful preview/diff, validate the operation and create a recoverable backup/snapshot/checkpoint before execution. If the required live-database backup cannot be created, the mutation MUST NOT proceed as though rollback exists.


For Data live-database changes, the approval surface SHOULD identify the intended operation, affected tables/entities/rows where knowable, schema/dependency impact, external side effects and backup identity. Execution MUST occur only after approval, then verify the actual result and preserve rollback/recovery information. Prior approval, Accept and Trust or Always Trust MUST NOT suppress this Data-specific per-action approval invariant.


Equivalent bar actions MUST behave consistently across product surfaces, while menus and available operations remain context-sensitive to the owning app. Unsupported or inapplicable actions MUST not be exposed merely to make the bar look feature-complete.

Home owns the reusable base component/service contract for the global persistent bottom AI bar required by interactive 9to1 apps. The shared component provides CUI rendering, Dulche connection, Universal Model Picker integration, permission/trust plumbing, request state and common Action Graph access.


Each host app MUST provide the bar with a permission-filtered semantic context snapshot and its typed supported actions. Home MUST NOT obtain app context through raw screen scraping when the host provides structured context. App-specific mutation semantics remain owned by the target app APIs.

sources.quote:
Cross-app invocation and compose contract
Every interactive 9to1 app that hosts the shared persistent AI bar MUST use Home's canonical compose invocation component and cross-app dispatcher. Plugins, Skills, Apps, Agents, Files and the reserved @Computer Use capability MUST therefore resolve consistently across apps rather than each product implementing a private @ syntax or resource picker.
A model may cross an app boundary only when that action is authorised by user intent: explicit @ invocation, an explicit instruction naming the target capability/app, or an unambiguous requested outcome whose canonical owner is another 9to1 app. Implied intent is semantic, not opportunistic; unrelated app access remains out of scope.
When a target 9to1 app owns the requested artifact/action, the originating model MUST use the target app's typed API/shared semantic action contract and MAY ask Home to launch/reveal the target app so the user can observe progress. For example, a request to create a presentation routes to Present and creates/edits a canonical Present artifact rather than fabricating a slide-like object in the originating app.
Computer Use MUST NOT be selected automatically as a fallback when typed app execution is unavailable, inconvenient or fails. It is usable only after explicit @Computer Use invocation and remains subject to the Computer Use eligibility, permission, game-exclusion and Autoreview rules.
Model-driven typed edits MAY be visualised in the target app with live object motion, selection highlights, text insertion and a synthetic/virtual cursor. This visualisation is not evidence that Dulche is literally controlling the pointer; the typed action/result remains authoritative and the synthetic cursor MUST be visually distinguishable from the user's actual input cursor.

The shared Home-owned floating AI compose component MUST provide one searchable @ invocation menu for Plugins, Skills, Apps, Agents and Files. The menu is a single interaction surface with collapsible type sections rather than separate unrelated pickers. Typing @ opens the resource list; typing text after @ filters across all sections while preserving each result's type and identity.
Selecting an item inserts an inline invocation chip/token inside the compose field at the caret position. The rendered token MUST display the resource's icon where available plus its human-readable label, for example an Agent may render as '@[agent icon] John'. The token MUST use a distinct invoked visual state, including colour/style differentiation, while also using non-colour cues for accessibility. Editing/deleting the token removes or changes the invocation rather than leaving invisible hidden attachment state.
Invocation tokens MUST store stable canonical identities, not only display text: Plugin PackageID/version or resolved active version, SkillID/version, AppID, AgentID/DefinitionRevision where required and File/Artifact reference identity/revision or access token as appropriate. Duplicate display names MUST therefore remain unambiguous. The resolved invocation set is included in request metadata, FullLog and Action Graph.
The Plugins section lists Dulche Plugins enabled/available in the current scope; Skills lists eligible Dulche Skills including the built-in Persistent Skill; Agents lists Agents available through Dulche scope resolution; Files searches authorised files/artifacts without silently granting new access. Availability in the picker never grants permission to execute protected actions or read inaccessible content.
The Apps section MUST contain every installed/available first-party 9to1 app plus user-installed applications that 9to1 can classify as safely operable through a typed API/integration or, when separately authorised, Computer Use. App entries MUST expose whether their interaction path is Typed/API, Computer Use Required, or both. Selecting an app whose only route is Computer Use MUST NOT activate Computer Use by itself; the request also requires the explicit @Computer Use invocation.
Game executables and anti-cheat-protected game surfaces MUST be excluded from the operable Apps invocation results even when discovered through Steam, Epic Games Launcher or another launcher/library. If 9to1 cannot confidently distinguish an eligible ordinary application from a game/anti-cheat target, it MUST omit or mark the target unavailable for Computer Use rather than risk automation. Play remains the supported Agent-game route defined by its own contract.
@Computer Use is a reserved first-party system capability entry in the same searchable invocation surface. Selecting it creates the explicit ComputerUseInvocationID required by the Dulche Computer Use contract and makes its active state visible in the compose field before the request is submitted.
Cross-app execution visualisation
Models operating inside any 9to1 app MAY invoke another 9to1 app only when the user's request explicitly names/invokes that app, directly asks for an outcome owned by that app, or unambiguously implies the owning app from the requested artifact/action. For example, 'create a presentation' resolves to Present; 'make a spreadsheet' resolves to Data; an unrelated app MUST NOT be opened merely because the model thinks it might be useful.
Cross-app intent resolution MUST bind to the owning app's stable AppID and typed capability contract. If the required app is not running, Home MAY launch/open it automatically when that is part of fulfilling the request. The target artifact remains canonical in its owning app, and the originating app/Space receives references/status rather than an unmanaged duplicate.
Typed app APIs and shared semantic actions are the normal execution path. Computer Use is not a fallback for missing/failed APIs and remains unavailable unless @Computer Use was explicitly invoked. Permission, review, edit/suggest/view state, conflicts and external-side-effect rules of the target app still apply to cross-app work.
Where an app has a visible editing surface, the user SHOULD be able to watch model-driven edits occur in real time. Home/shared app infrastructure MUST provide an execution-visualisation stream that maps semantic actions to visible UI changes such as objects moving, text appearing, selections changing, slides being created or a virtual cursor hovering over the affected target.
The execution visualiser is representational, not the control mechanism. A virtual cursor MUST be visually distinguishable from the user's real pointer and MUST NOT generate mouse/keyboard input merely to make the animation believable. The canonical typed API/action result remains authoritative; visual animation follows confirmed/provisional semantic events and MUST reconcile to final app state after errors, retries or rollback.

requirements.requirement: P1 — Shared Productivity Engine cross-app schemas, editing and bundles

sources.quote:
Home owns the Shared Productivity Engine used by Write, Present, Canvas, Boards and Spaces for overlapping document/object behaviours. The engine is a shared canonical object/rendering/action layer, not five copied implementations. App shells MAY provide different workflows and layout chrome, but a shared object type MUST use the same schema, formatting semantics, rendering rules and typed object actions wherever that type is supported.


The initial required shared object families include rich text/paragraphs, headings, lists/checklists, code blocks, equations, tables, images/media, drawings/ink, graph objects and typed embedded 9to1 artifact references. The registry MUST be extensible so a new shared object type can be implemented once and enabled in multiple supporting surfaces without rewriting its core editor/renderer.


App-specific document structures remain allowed. Present still owns slides and presentation-level layout; Canvas still owns its infinite spatial surface; Boards owns Board/Page hierarchy and Board-specific layout. The shared engine standardises reusable embedded/shared objects rather than forcing one top-level document model.


Canonical object identity, schemas and style registry


Every shared object instance MUST have a stable ObjectID within its owning artifact plus a versioned ObjectType/schema identifier. Object content, formatting, accessibility metadata, asset references and app-neutral layout properties MUST be serialisable independently from transient UI state. Unknown required schema versions MUST fail explicitly rather than being silently flattened or reinterpreted.


Shared object schemas MUST preserve enough information for semantically identical rendering/editing across participating apps. If an app cannot support a property, it MUST retain that property in the object payload when round-tripping and surface the limitation instead of destructively stripping it.


The engine MUST provide a shared versioned style registry for reusable text/paragraph/object style definitions. Style definitions use stable StyleID identity independent of display name so renaming a style does not detach existing objects. App-specific style extensions MAY exist but MUST preserve shared base properties when transferred.

The engine MUST provide a versioned ProductivityObjectBundle clipboard/transfer format containing shared object payloads, style definitions, asset references, accessibility metadata and a portable fallback representation. Copying a supported object from one participating app and pasting it into another MUST preserve the same shared-object semantics and appearance rather than converting it to an image or lossy app-specific approximation.


When the destination supports the same shared object type, paste creates/imports a native shared object instance using the same schema. When the destination does not support that object type but supports embedded 9to1 artifacts, the UI MUST offer an embed/reference path. Destructive flattening is allowed only as an explicit export/paste-as-static action.


Spaces MUST use the Shared Productivity Engine for rich pasted/embedded content so tables, code blocks, drawings, graphs and other shared objects preserve their structure instead of degrading to plain text. Spaces may present a conversational shell around the object, but editing MUST route through the same shared object actions.


Rendering, editing, undo and actions


The engine MUST provide shared selection, focus, formatting, object insertion/removal, resize/transform where applicable, clipboard, accessibility and undoable action primitives for shared object types. Shared actions MUST have stable typed representations so compatible apps can participate in undo/recovery and AI/Automation execution without reproducing hidden per-app commands.


App-specific shells MAY add contextual commands, but MUST NOT fork the underlying object semantics into incompatible versions. Object actions MUST be exposed through typed APIs and usable by UI, Spaces, Automations and Dulche-driven AI without raw UI simulation.


The shared engine MUST emit semantic selection/context information for the persistent AI bar and app-specific contextual toolbars. This context MUST contain stable object/selection identity rather than requiring consumers to infer meaning from rendered pixels.


Drawing engine


The shared engine MUST expose the Rnote-derived drawing/ink engine as a reusable shared object/layer so Canvas and Boards use the same stroke model, pen/eraser behaviours and serialisation primitives. Other productivity surfaces MAY opt into the same drawing object without implementing a separate ink stack.


Deployment boundary and compatibility


Home Core MUST expose the Shared Productivity Engine as a versioned shared platform capability. Apps may link/embed approved shared engine libraries/components as part of their package for rendering performance, but the canonical schema registry, compatibility negotiation and shared service/version authority remain Home-owned. Apps MUST validate compatible engine/schema versions during startup.


Shared object schemas and ProductivityObjectBundle MUST be versioned independently of individual app versions. Home MUST expose compatibility negotiation so an older app can detect a newer unsupported shared object type/property before editing. Compatible unknown optional properties MUST be preserved; incompatible required features MUST produce a structured compatibility state rather than silent data loss.

The above are minimum cross-app entry points. Each shared object type MUST also expose its typed creation/update/query actions through the owning app/API surface required by the global API-parity rule.

requirements.requirement: P0 — MCP client/server lifecycle, schemas, permissions and recovery

sources.quote:
MCP is a first-class Dulche extension/runtime capability. Dulche MUST support acting as an MCP client for authorised local/remote MCP servers and acting as an MCP server when 9-1 intentionally exposes approved capabilities to external MCP clients. MCP execution MUST use the same permission, audit, cancellation, timeout and structured-error contracts as native Dulche tools.


Identity and lifecycle


Every configured MCP connection MUST have a stable ServerID independent of display name or transport address. Configuration MUST record role (client/server), transport/process/endpoint definition, credential references, trust state, capability snapshot/version and owner/scope. Credentials MUST be stored by secure reference and MUST NOT be embedded as plaintext in project manifests or logs.


Client connections MUST expose at least Disconnected, Connecting, Ready, Degraded, Reconnecting, Failed and Stopped states. Reconnect MUST NOT replay a previously completed consequential tool call. A broken connection returns structured transport/provider failures and MUST NOT be reported as Ready.


Capability discovery and schemas


Dulche MUST discover and represent the capabilities actually exposed by an MCP server, including tools and, where supported by the negotiated MCP version/server, resources and prompts. Tool input/output schemas MUST be validated before dispatch/consumption. Capability changes MUST invalidate stale cached schemas before later calls use them.


Capability identity is server-scoped: two MCP servers MAY expose the same human-readable tool name without collision because the canonical identity includes ServerID plus capability identity/name. User-facing aliases MAY exist but MUST NOT replace stable server-scoped identity.


Permissions and execution


Connecting to an MCP server does not authorise all capabilities it exposes. Each tool/resource capability MUST resolve through Dulche/Home permission and risk evaluation according to its effective read/write/external-side-effect scope. Server-provided descriptions/content MUST NOT grant permissions, alter trust state or override caller restrictions.


MCP tool execution MUST support cancellation/timeouts when supported by the active transport/server and MUST record when cancellation is best-effort or too late because an external action already completed. Results, approvals, failures, blockers and side effects MUST appear in ToolLog, AuditLog, FullLog and Action Graph like equivalent native tools.

Unsupported capabilities MUST return UnsupportedCapability rather than fabricated empty results. Protocol-version-specific functionality MAY extend this API while preserving compatibility with the stable core.


Tool Builder integration and acceptance


MCP projects produced by AI Studio Tool Builder MUST validate against the same Dulche MCP connection/schema/permission contract used at runtime. MCP support is implementation-complete only when local and remote connections can be configured, discovered, permissioned, called, cancelled/failed, reconnected and audited without bespoke per-app wiring, and when approved 9-1 capabilities can be exposed through server mode without bypassing their original permission model.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Skill/Plugin package identity, separated enablement and transactional updates

sources.quote:
Skills and Plugins are separate first-class Dulche extension types. A Skill packages reusable instructions, workflows, context rules and resources for model/Agent/Harness execution. A Plugin packages executable or integrated capabilities and MAY expose typed tools/actions, CUI surfaces or external-service functionality. Neither type is interchangeable with MCP, although a Skill or Plugin MAY declare an MCP dependency.


Common package contract


Every Skill and Plugin MUST have a versioned manifest containing stable PackageID, package type, version, minimum/compatible Dulche versions, provenance/origin, declared capabilities, required/requested permissions, dependencies, entry points/resources, update metadata and integrity/signature information when the distribution channel supports signing. Display name MUST NOT be used as package identity.


Manifest parsing and dependency resolution MUST be deterministic. Unknown required manifest fields/capabilities block installation or enablement with a structured compatibility failure; unknown optional fields MAY be preserved for forward compatibility. Packages MUST NOT execute code merely because their manifest was inspected or imported.


Lifecycle, trust and permissions


Installation, enablement, permissions and trust are separate states. Installing a package registers its files/manifest but MUST NOT automatically enable it for every caller, grant requested permissions, connect external accounts or grant Accept and Always Trust. Enablement only makes the package available within the selected scope; individual actions still use the normal Dulche/Home permission and risk model.


Package lifecycle MUST expose at least Installed, Disabled, Enabled, Updating, Failed and Quarantined states. A package that fails integrity/signature/compatibility validation MUST NOT become Enabled. Quarantine preserves evidence/metadata needed for diagnosis while preventing execution.


Updates MUST be version-aware and transactional. Dulche MUST validate/stage the new version and dependency graph before switching the active version. Failure during update MUST leave the previous known-good version available when rollback is technically possible. Package updates MUST NOT silently expand effective permissions; newly requested scopes require a new permission decision.


Uninstall MUST define what happens to package-owned persistent data. Shared/user-authored data MUST NOT be silently deleted merely because a package is removed. Orphaned package state MAY be retained for recovery/reinstall according to explicit retention policy.


Skill model


A Skill is primarily declarative. It MAY contain instructions, workflow definitions, templates/prompts, context-selection rules, examples, resources/files and references to permitted tools/Plugins/MCP capabilities. A Skill MUST NOT gain arbitrary code execution solely by being a Skill; executable behaviour requires an explicitly declared/authorised executable extension capability such as a Plugin/tool dependency.


Skill activation MUST be explicit and observable in request/run metadata. Dulche MUST record which Skill IDs/versions contributed to a request so Result provenance, logs and Action Graph can identify the active Skill set. Conflicting or incompatible Skills MUST resolve through a deterministic precedence/compatibility rule or return Conflict; Dulche MUST NOT silently merge contradictory required policies.


Built-in Persistent skill
Dulche MUST ship a first-party built-in Skill with the canonical display name Persistent and a stable reserved SkillID. Activating Persistent on a request sets that root request's PersistencePolicy to Persistent. The Skill is declarative: it changes Runtime orchestration semantics and does not gain permissions, tools, external access, budget or trust merely by being active.
Persistent activation MUST be explicit and visible in request metadata, the compose invocation state, FullLog and Action Graph. It MAY be invoked through the shared @ resource picker as @Persistent. The active version MUST be recorded like every other Skill so later inspection can prove which persistence contract governed the run.
The Persistent Skill MUST use the canonical Dulche persistent-request contract. In particular, an ordinary checkpoint, context compaction boundary, provider lease expiry, model restart, recoverable tool timeout or similar continuation boundary MUST NOT be treated as successful completion of the turn. The Runtime preserves/reconstructs execution state and continues under the same RootRequestID until the task's completion criteria are actually satisfied, the user explicitly stops it, or all remaining work is non-terminally AwaitingUser because of an unresolved blocker.
While a Persistent turn is running, an ordinary follow-up message sent by the user MUST join the same root turn as a SteeringMessage and MUST NOT implicitly cancel, replace or interrupt the active work. Dulche consumes the message at the next safe planning boundary, updates the plan and continues. Explicit Stop, explicit replace/edit semantics and any separately exposed interrupt/stack action retain their distinct meanings.
A blocker that cannot be resolved within the request's effective permission and capability bounds MUST be surfaced to the user as a structured blocker immediately. The blocker MUST isolate only the dependent work. Dulche MUST continue any independent runnable work in the same persistent turn; if no independent work remains, the turn enters AwaitingUser without being misreported as complete or timed out. When the blocker is resolved, the same durable turn resumes from current state rather than silently restarting completed work.
Persistent MUST remain compatible with automatic context compaction, Context Summarisation, Subagents, checkpoints, crash recovery and provider/model fallback. None of those mechanisms may erase completed side-effect evidence, duplicate consequential actions or weaken permission/approval requirements.
Plugin model


A Plugin MAY expose typed tools/actions, external-service connectors and optional CUI surfaces. Every exposed callable capability MUST declare input/output schemas, permission scopes, risk/side-effect classification and cancellation/timeout semantics where applicable. Plugin tool calls MUST enter the same ToolLog, AuditLog, FullLog and Action Graph pipeline as native tools and MCP calls.


Plugin CUI surfaces MUST render through approved CUI contracts and MUST NOT inject arbitrary trusted application code/markup outside the declared host surface. A Plugin surface does not inherit permission to invoke its Plugin’s actions without the applicable caller/user permission grants.
