requirements.requirement: P0 — External integrations shared Connection, provider scopes and account identity

sources.quote:
A provider account should be connected once through the integration framework and then reused by authorised 9to1 surfaces. Consuming apps MUST request capabilities from the existing Connection rather than maintaining private duplicate credentials or running their own hidden authentication flows.
Examples include a Google connection supplying Drive capabilities to Files, Gmail capabilities to Mail, Calendar capabilities to Planner/Calendar and Contacts capabilities to relevant people pickers; a GitHub connection may supply repository/issue/pull-request capabilities to Stack, Dev or authorised Dulche Agents. The exact provider capabilities available remain determined by granted provider scopes and the integration adapter.
Provider scope versus 9to1 permission
Provider authorisation and 9to1 authorisation are separate gates. A Connection may possess provider scopes that a particular app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension is not authorised to use. Both the remote provider scope and the applicable 9to1 permission/capability policy MUST allow an operation before it is executed.
Connecting an account MUST NOT implicitly grant every 9to1 surface unrestricted access to that account. Permission decisions should be made at an appropriate capability/resource scope and remain inspectable/revocable.
Typed capability contracts
Consuming apps SHOULD depend on provider-neutral typed capabilities where equivalent semantics exist instead of embedding provider-specific endpoint logic. Examples include Files.List/Read/Upload, Mail.Search/Read/Send, Calendar.ListEvents/CreateEvent, Contacts.Search, Git.ListRepositories/CreateIssue and Chat.ListMessages or equivalent canonical contracts.
Provider adapters map those typed capabilities onto the provider's API. Provider-specific features that cannot be represented faithfully through a common contract may be exposed through explicit provider-namespaced capabilities; the common abstraction MUST NOT silently discard important provider semantics merely to force false parity.
Capability schemas MUST declare input/output shape, supported operations, required provider scopes, relevant 9to1 permissions, pagination/streaming behaviour, provider limitations and error states.
Authentication and credential storage
The integration framework centrally owns supported authentication flows such as OAuth/OIDC, PKCE, device-code flows, API-key authentication or provider-specific enterprise methods where appropriate. Apps MUST NOT request or persist reusable provider credentials directly when the integration framework can broker them.
Credential material such as access tokens, refresh tokens, API keys, passwords and private keys MUST live in approved secure credential storage. Integration records, Den records, logs, exports and app settings store credential references/connection identities rather than plaintext reusable secrets.
Token refresh, expiry, revocation and provider reauthentication are lifecycle concerns of the integration framework. A consumer receives a capability result or typed authentication-required failure, not raw credentials it can reuse arbitrarily.
Scope escalation
If a Connection exists but lacks a provider scope required by a new capability, the consuming surface requests scope escalation through the shared integration framework. The user must be shown which additional provider access is being requested and why. The framework extends/replaces the existing authorisation where the provider supports it rather than creating a hidden duplicate connection.
Remote identity and canonical 9to1 entities
External objects MUST retain their remote identity and provenance. A RemoteEntityReference should identify the provider, Connection, remote object ID, remote revision/version where available, remote URL/reference and any mapped canonical 9to1 entity.
Opening or referencing a remote object does not automatically create a separate canonical copy. The UI and APIs MUST distinguish operations such as Open remote, Import/copy into 9to1, Link/reference and Keep synchronised.
Where an external object is mapped to a canonical 9to1 entity, the relationship must remain explicit so the system does not create multiple disconnected local copies of the same remote item or accidentally treat provider IDs as globally unique without Connection/provider context.

Dulche and Agent access
Dulche, Agents and AI surfaces use External App Integrations through the same typed capabilities and permissions as first-party apps. Dulche does not own a parallel account-authentication layer.
For example, a request to find an email uses an authorised Mail capability for an existing connection; a request to create a GitHub issue uses the relevant Git capability. Normal Dulche tool/action permissions and consequential-action confirmation requirements still apply. Merely connecting an account does not grant every Agent permission to mutate it.
Relationship to Plugins and MCP
External App Integrations, Plugins and MCP are distinct abstractions. External App Integrations represent durable authenticated third-party account/service relationships and their capabilities. Plugins are installable packages that may add executable/integrated functionality. MCP is a protocol by which Dulche can discover/use tools/resources.
They may interoperate: a Plugin may register a provider adapter; an integration capability may be surfaced to Dulche through an approved tool/MCP bridge. Such composition MUST preserve the underlying Connection identity, provider scopes and 9to1 permission checks rather than laundering authority through another abstraction.
Provider SDK and extension
9to1 SHOULD expose a versioned Integration Provider SDK/manifest contract so additional providers can be implemented without changing every consuming app. A provider definition can declare provider identity/branding metadata, authentication method, capability schemas, provider scopes, remote entity types, webhook/change-feed support, rate-limit semantics, health checks and provider-specific settings.
Third-party provider adapters remain sandboxed/permissioned according to their implementation model. Registering a provider does not grant unrestricted access to other Connections, credential stores or unrelated local data.
Disconnect and revocation
Disconnect semantics MUST be explicit and predictable. Disconnecting a Connection should stop sync/background activity, invalidate or remove local credential references as appropriate, disable provider capabilities and clear/expire caches according to policy. Where supported and requested, provider-side token revocation should also be attempted.
Disconnecting an account MUST NOT automatically delete unrelated local 9to1 artifacts previously imported from it. For linked/synchronised objects, the UI must explain what local data remains, what becomes unavailable and whether any pending remote operations are abandoned.
Security invariants
* Possessing a provider credential does not grant any app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension unrestricted access to the associated account.
* Every external operation must pass both provider scope/capability validation and the relevant 9to1 permission boundary.
* Consuming apps receive capability access/results, not raw reusable credentials.
* Connection/account identity, remote-object identity, provenance and provider limitations must remain explicit across app boundaries.
* Logs, exports and Den records must not contain plaintext reusable provider secrets.

Sync, webhooks and change feeds
Where a provider supports webhooks, push notifications or incremental change feeds, the integration framework SHOULD use them rather than each app independently polling the same account. It owns webhook registration/renewal/validation, change cursors, deduplication, retry/backoff and background refresh.

Consumers may continue to display authorised cached state while a provider is unavailable, but the stale/offline state and last successful sync/freshness information MUST remain visible when material. The framework MUST NOT silently claim remote mutations succeeded when they have only been queued locally.
If queued remote writes are supported, each operation needs stable identity, retry/idempotency semantics, dependency ordering where applicable, visible pending/failed state and explicit conflict handling. Reconnection must not blindly replay an action that is no longer valid or that already completed remotely.

For synchronised/mirrored objects, use provider revision identifiers, ETags/version tokens or equivalent change metadata where available. Wall-clock timestamps alone MUST NOT be the only conflict authority.

Provider-side deletion, permission loss and remote moves/renames require explicit typed states rather than being treated as generic missing-file errors.

Connections expose typed health/lifecycle states such as Connected, AuthenticationRequired, ScopeRequired, RateLimited, ProviderUnavailable, Degraded, SyncError, Revoked and Disabled or equivalent. Apps consume these states and present appropriate user-facing recovery rather than leaking raw HTTP/provider exceptions.
Health information should include the failing capability/provider account where relevant, last successful contact/sync, retryability and the action required from the user when one exists.

The shared layer MUST centrally support pagination, retry-after handling, provider quotas, transient network retries, exponential backoff/jitter, idempotency, request cancellation, partial response handling and provider-specific service limits. Consuming apps MUST NOT each invent incompatible retry/quota behaviour.

9to1 MUST provide a central integrations management surface, hosted under the appropriate Home/Settings area, showing provider, connected account identity, connection status, provider-granted scopes/capabilities, authorised 9to1 consumers where exposed, recent/last successful activity, errors, reconnect/re-authorise, permission management and disconnect/revoke actions.

requirements.requirement: P0 — Computer Use explicit opt-in, target authority and hard exclusions

sources.quote:
Computer Use is a first-class Dulche capability but MUST be opt-in per request. It is enabled only by an explicit @Computer Use invocation token or an equivalent explicit user control that resolves to the same ComputerUseInvocationID. An ordinary natural-language request, an @App mention or failure of a typed app API MUST NOT silently activate Computer Use.
The Computer Use capability may control eligible graphical applications through supported pointer, keyboard, accessibility/automation and visual-interaction primitives. It SHOULD use the fastest reliable state channel available, including accessibility/automation metadata where appropriate, avoid unnecessary human-speed delays, batch safe independent interactions where supported and verify state transitions instead of relying on fixed sleeps. Speed MUST NOT weaken verification or permission gates.
By default, the first attempted interaction with each target application in a Computer Use run requires user approval for that AppID/process identity, and changes to application or operating-system settings require approval before mutation. Home settings MUST allow the user to change this policy to automatic approval for eligible apps and to an Approve All eligible-apps policy. Persisted approval policy remains scoped by user/profile, app identity and the normal Home trust/permission model.
Auto-approve and Approve All MUST NOT bypass hard exclusions, administrator policy, OS security boundaries or other non-overridable safeguards. Computer Use receives no more filesystem, network, credential, settings or app authority than the invoking user/request already possesses.
Generic Computer Use MUST NOT attach to, send input to, automate or manipulate game executables or anti-cheat-protected game surfaces, including games launched or managed through platforms such as Steam or Epic Games Launcher. When classification is uncertain and anti-cheat/game automation risk is plausible, the target is ineligible by default. This exclusion exists independently of user trust level because generic automation can create account/anti-cheat risk.
The game exclusion does not prohibit Dulche Agents from participating in games deliberately configured through the 9to1 Play framework. Play interaction MUST occur through Play's typed GameDefinition/Match/contestant actions and capability isolation, not by using generic Computer Use to drive an external game client.
Every Computer Use run MUST produce an inspectable action stream with target app/window identity, action type, timestamps, relevant pre/post state evidence, approvals, failures and side effects. Sensitive screen regions, credentials and typed secrets MUST follow the normal redaction and permission rules; logs MUST NOT become a second plaintext credential store.
Dulche Autoreview MUST inspect proposed and recent Computer Use actions continuously. It MUST flag patterns including repeated identical or near-identical actions without progress, repeated failing commands, oscillation between states, privilege escalation, bulk/destructive deletion, destructive shell commands such as rm -rf or platform equivalents, security-setting changes, suspicious executable/download flows and other high-risk sequences. High-confidence imminent destructive risk MUST be able to pause the next action for review rather than merely add a passive warning.
Autoreview findings are structured ProblemEvents and MUST feed the shared Problem handling contract. A Computer Use recovery intervention MUST preserve the current request, state and logs and SHOULD redirect to a safer or more direct interaction strategy. It MUST NOT hide that a risky action was proposed or attempted.

Verify authorised targets against the actual process/window/session before dispatch, and revalidate after relevant focus or target changes. Fix integration failures without disabling permission checks. Combine actual screenshots with structured accessibility/control information; a text control tree is not a screenshot, and successful dispatch or readback alone is not outcome verification. Test the requested effects in the real application, including persistence and reopening where relevant.
Provide reliable supported click types, double-click, drag, scroll, typing and shortcuts, with correct multi-monitor coordinates and display scaling. Avoid unintended focus, clipboard and held-key/button changes; restore temporary clipboard use only when doing so will not overwrite newer user content. Detect user takeover and yield rather than competing for input. Describe shared-desktop versus isolated-session limits honestly; a decorative virtual pointer is not independent input isolation.
Use a reusable native execution service or equivalent rather than unnecessary per-action process startup. Support bounded planned action sequences with target checks, interruption points and appropriate readbacks; do not require a model turn per predictable action. requirements.requirement: P1 — Shared Problem detection, manual reporting and bounded recovery

sources.quote:
Problem handling is a first-class Dulche Runtime capability for detecting, surfacing and recovering from common model/agent failure modes without forcing every app to implement its own ad-hoc watchdog.
The canonical ProblemType set MUST support at least Looping, NoProgress/Stuck, Repetition, HallucinationOrFabrication, OverAgreement/Sycophancy, InstructionDrift, ContradictionWithGroundedState, RepeatedToolFailure, UnsafeActionPattern and Other/UserReported. Additional typed categories MAY be added versionably without collapsing distinct existing meanings.
Loop detection MUST consider semantic and action-level repetition, not only identical text. Examples include repeatedly issuing the same failing command, alternately undoing/reapplying the same mutation, reopening the same surface without new evidence, recreating completed work or repeatedly restating the same answer while the task remains unfinished.
Hallucination/fabrication detection SHOULD use available grounded evidence such as tool results, canonical app state, source provenance, stable object IDs and completion evidence. Dulche MUST flag fabricated claims of completed actions, nonexistent files/entities/tool results or unsupported factual assertions when confidence is sufficient; it MUST NOT treat disagreement with an unverified model statement as proof that the user is wrong.
OverAgreement/Sycophancy detection SHOULD flag responses that materially adopt or endorse a user's factual premise, conclusion or requested assessment without adequate evidence when the task calls for grounded evaluation. Recovery prompts the model to re-evaluate the evidence and user request; it MUST NOT mechanically disagree with the user merely to appear independent.
When automatic detection reaches its configured intervention threshold, Dulche creates a ProblemEvent and injects a clearly identified Runtime recovery directive at the next safe boundary. The directive tells the model what failure pattern was detected, relevant evidence and the required correction, such as stop repeating the command, reassess grounded state, use a different strategy or verify the claimed result. Runtime recovery directives MUST NOT be forged as user-authored messages.
If the detected problem is associated with a proposed consequential or dangerous tool/Computer Use action, Dulche MAY pause dispatch before the action and require re-planning or applicable approval. requirements.requirement: P0 — Tool-call whole-unit batching and reconciliation efficiency

sources.quote:
Optimise time and cost to a verified result, not tool-call volume. Apply to all agents, including ordinary chat models performing agentic work, Assistants, Specialists and delegated workers. Default to: probe when uncertain → plan the whole work unit → batch execute → verify → repair. Do not insert fresh model reasoning between predictable individual operations.


Probe only when needed — Read the relevant tool contract and reuse verified knowledge for the same tool/version/environment. If behaviour is unfamiliar or uncertain, run a minimal, reversible representative test: one object, or the smallest batch needed to check bulk behaviour. Inspect actual units, axes, placement, scale, rotation, asset references and returned IDs as applicable. Delete only the test objects using their recorded IDs and confirm cleanup before production work. Prefer safe staging or dry-run support where available. Repeat probes only when relevant assumptions change; a successful small probe does not establish large-batch capacity.


Plan the whole work unit — Design the complete building, track or other coherent deliverable before executing its repetitive operations. Prepare a deterministic operation manifest containing the assets, transforms/parameters, dependencies, expected outputs and checks; validate it before submission. Generate repetitive data programmatically where supported instead of individually reasoning through each item. Revise the plan when new evidence, failures or user steering require it, not after every successful operation.


Batch execution — Submit the complete validated work unit in one supported bulk call when safe. Otherwise use bounded chunks, or a supported authorised script/executor that runs the planned calls without a model turn per item. Do not invent a bulk endpoint or assume every MCP supports batching. Where no suitable executor exists, use the available calls efficiently and disclose the constraint rather than claiming a batch occurred. Preserve dependency ordering; parallelise only independent operations that the service can safely process.


Adaptive limits — Choose batch size from known or measured payload, timeout, rate, memory, recovery and responsiveness limits. Start conservatively when capacity is unknown, increase after successful observations and reduce or change approach after failures. Do not jump from one successful test object to 50,000 untested placements. Keep execution interruptible at supported safe boundaries so steering, pause and cancellation remain effective. Batching never expands permissions or bypasses per-action approval requirements.


Verify and recover — Check results after each logical batch or bounded chunk using actual state readback and appropriate visual inspection; verify the assembled result against the manifest and acceptance criteria. For a map, inspect the actual scene from useful views and test relevant traversal/collision behaviour, not merely the reported object count. A successful tool response or sampled visual check alone does not verify the whole deliverable. Repair affected items and rerun relevant checks. Track per-item outcomes and created IDs; after partial failure or timeout, reconcile actual state before retrying, preserve successful work and avoid duplicates. Roll back only identified task-owned changes where safe, never unrelated user work.


Avoid redundant overhead — Reuse current schemas, asset lookups and unchanged results; refresh when invalidated or freshness matters. Batch related reads, request only needed fields and keep large manifests/logs outside repeated model context, with concise summaries and retrievable evidence. Avoid per-object screenshots, explanations, schema rediscovery and busy polling when batch-level evidence suffices. Record real batch/checkpoint progress in the existing dashboard without turning every object into a checkpoint. Efficiency must never weaken quality, required checks or the final verification gate.

Tool-efficiency release checks: demonstrate unfamiliar-tool probing and cleanup, reuse of valid tool knowledge, whole-unit planning, supported batching/chunking without per-object replanning, visual and functional verification, partial-failure recovery without duplicates, and steering at safe boundaries. Compare elapsed time, model turns and tool round trips with a per-item baseline on the same representative task and acceptance tests; efficiency gains must preserve output quality and verification coverage.
